Cost of Living—Economic Policy and Reports
1. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance: What
steps is the Government taking to keep down the cost of living for New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has taken a number
of steps and, assisted by general economic conditions, is helping to keep interest rates at
50-year lows and annual inflation at around 1 percent. The steps the Government has
taken are to maintain a track to surplus, which will take the pressure off interest rates
and reduce inflation pressures; responsible  and orthodox monetary policy is helping
keep inflation low; increased competition in  the electricity indus try has halved the 8
percent annual increase in electricity prices  in the 9 years up to 2008; cutting red tape
and increasing flexibility for businesses m eans better prices for customers; and
investing in infrastructure and delivering better public services helps the economy
become more competitive.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What recent reports has he received on the cost of living?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One measure of the cost of living is the Consumers Price
Index. Statistics New Zealand today reports th at consumer prices rose by 0.4 percent in
the March quarter, and annual inflation—that is , the inflation for the year up to the end
of March—was 0.9 percent. This means that an nual inflation has now been running at 1
percent or less for four quarter s. This is well down on inflat ion of more than 5 percent
per annum, which was the rate when the Government took office in late 2008. The
impact of low inflation on interest rates means that a family with a $200,000 mortgage
is around $200 a week better off in interest payments compared with late 2008.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What reports has he received on recent food prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The food price index came out last week for March. Of
course, food prices fluctuate, often for seas onal reasons as much as for cost and price
inflation reasons. This report showed that f ood prices fell in the month of March. Food
prices for the year to March, which encompasses the whole seasonal cycle, fell by 0.4
percent—that is, on average, food prices for the year to March went down.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: How do these moderate cost of living increases compare with
increases in real after-tax wages?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, these moderate increa ses and, of course, for some
classes of expenditure such as food, reductions in the co st of living compare quite
favourably with wage increases in the last  5 years. Since September 2008 gross wages
9430 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Apr 2013
have increased by 14 percent. After tax they have increased by 22 percent. Inflation has
been 9 percent, which means that real af ter-tax wages have increased by 12 percent
since September 2008. In the 9 years up to September 2008, after-tax wages increased
by only 4 percent.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is it correct that power prices went up by 5.2 percent to 31 March,
which is nearly six times the rate of inflation? Can he confirm that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I will take the member at his word. That price increase is
included in the collect ive CPI, which went up by 0.9 pe rcent for the year. So some
households would have paid more for electricity and they paid less for food; on balance,
their cost of living went up by 0.9 percent. But all households are grateful the Labour
Government is no longer in charge—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! That is quite a sufficient answer, thank
you.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Well, can he explain, then, how k eeping ACC levies artificially high
keeps down the cost of living for New Zealanders when the regulatory impact statement
on this decision shows that the Government’s  refusal to lower levies, as recommended
by ACC and the Ministry of Business, Innova tion and Employment, is costing workers
and employers up to $2 billion more a year than what is needed to cover the cost of
injuries?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: That is a bit rich coming from the party that expanded
entitlement to ACC without increasing the le vies, but I agree with the member. If we
can continue to reduce ACC levies, it will re duce the cost of living. Two years ago we
did decrease those levies by $600 million per year, and we are looking at every
opportunity to decrease them further.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: How does increasing fuel taxes by 9c a litre keep the cost of
living down, especially given that transport officials advised the Government that an
increase of that magnitude would raise nearly  $20 billion more than  what is required to
carry out their road-building programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I do not agree at all with  the member’s last assertion.
In fact, the fuel tax is calibrated to the roading investment programme in a highly
transparent manner. That fuel tax increase is  part of the collective measure of price
increases, the CPI, which shows that over the last year the cost of  living went up by 1
percent. I hope Labour keeps going on about this issue, because the more it complains
about the rise in the cost of living, the lower it seems to be.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I seek leave to table two tables from a briefing received by the
Minister of Transport from the ministry that indicate that fuel excise taxes of 9c a litre
will generate nearly $20 billion more than required.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table those tw o tables. Is there any objection?
There appears to be none. They can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Prime Minister—Statements on Power Prices and Government Communications
Security Bureau
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “We’ve done as good a job as
we can in the conditions we’ve got to try and help low-inco me New Zealanders.”; if so,
does he think power bills going up by six ti mes the rate of inflation will help low-
income families?
17 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9431

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. I think it is worth recalling the track record of this
Government, which has seen power prices go up by about 20 percent in our time in
office, compared with the 72 percent incr ease under Labour. But I have no doubt that
the little Labour elves will be trying to dream something up to back up their—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. He did answer the question
when he said yes. I do not think he needed to go on.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: He did, and I certainly agree with that, and on that basis we will call
a supplementary question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that he has been in power now for more than 4½ years, can he
guarantee to consumers that electricity prices wi ll not increase further as a result of the
asset sales programme, given that power pr ices have gone up by six times more than
inflation?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not believe that the mi xed-ownership model programme
will have any influence on the prices that co nsumers pay. It is actually not true that
State-owned enterprises offer cheaper prices than private companies. The most recent
information I have shows that Contact En ergy, the largest privately owned company,
has the lowest national weighted average price for electricity of any retailer.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Given that electricity prices in creased more rapidly than in our
competitor countries over the last 4 years, at a time when electricity demand is flat, does
he think the electricity market is work ing for the benefit of hard-working New
Zealanders?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is certainly working a lot be tter than it was. Let us face
facts. Prices went up by 72 percent unde r Labour. This Government has actually
reformed the electricity sector with some  very significant moves, including closing
Whirinaki and including virtual swaps that have taken place. The truth is that on
Monday, to get in the paper, David Shearer said he would keep power prices down. He
has got no clue how to do that. The little Labour elves are trying to work out how to
make that happen, and it will not.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The only person without a clue,
as we found out yesterday, is the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a point of order.  It is not a point of order, but I
invite the member to ask a supplementary question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Has his Minister for Social Development told him that requests to
Work and Income for grants to pay for elect ricity and for gas tripled in the 2-year
period; if so, does he intend to take any action to bring down electricity prices for
ordinary, hard-working New Zealanders?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, the Government has ta ken action, and that is why the
rate of power increases is going up slower  under a National Government than under a
Labour Government. Secondly, the Government , in very difficult economic times, has
provided tremendous support for at-risk New Zealanders, and will continue to do so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Twenty-four hours after first being asked how many phone
calls he made to Ian Flet cher prior to his appoint ment as the Government
Communications Security Bureau head, what is his answer?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The right honourable Prime Minister , as far as it relates to the
primary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The same answer I gave yesterday: I do not have that
information with me. If the member wants to put it down in writing, my office will
provide it to him.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Any Prime Minister
would realise after yesterday’s answer that  that was never going to be satisfactory.
9432 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Apr 2013
Twenty-four hours later he turns up here a nd he does not know the answer to a very
critically serious question. That is just a cover-up.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The difficulty with the situation here is that it was a very
general primary question. Many Speakers have ruled that it is inappropriate to demand
an exacting answer to a supplementary quest ion that follows a very general primary
question. The Prime Minister has given you wh at I think is a satisfactory course of
action—for you to put down a more specific question at the next question time.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The difference between
one and two, which is the question here, I think—whether ther e was one phone call
made to Mr Fletcher by the Prime Minister or two—is not really exacting. I mean, it is
100 percent different. Anyone would remember  whether they made one or two phone
calls.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the comment the member is making. It is for the Prime
Minister to determine how he  has decided to answer the question, and he has answered
it in the way that he has. That has addressed the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why does the Prime Minister not treat this House seriously
and get his staff to trawl through his phone records for the period prior to Mr Ian
Fletcher’s appointment, and come to this  House and answer frankly, openly, and
properly, the way former Prime Ministers have done?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member has two options: put it down as a primary
question, and I will give him the answer, or put  it down in writing, and my office will
give him the answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Given his previous statements about intelligence matters,
did the SIS tell him about the residency application of a man by the name of Kim Vestor
when he met with them on 12 October 2010, one  day before the SIS, strangely, blocked
the man’s application?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I seek leave to table an affidavit of Grant Kenneth
Wormald for first defendant in relation to minutes, 28 September 2012, in the Kim
Dotcom case.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that affidav it. Is there any objection? Is it a
matter that has been before the courts and th en been released by the courts, or does it
breach any—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Released.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It has been released, I am assured. I therefore put the leave. Leave is
sought to table that affidavit. Is there any objection? There appears to be none. It can be
so tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Resource Management Act—Business Investment and Proposed Reforms
3. AARON GILMORE (National)  to the Minister for the Environment : What
recent reports has she seen on the impact  of the Resource Management Act 1991 on
business investment in New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Earlier this week Statistics
New Zealand published its 2012 Business Operati ons Survey. It shows that in the last 2
years hundreds of New Zealand businesses ha ve cancelled projects  worth potentially
$800 million to our economy, due mostly not to the standards that they have to meet but
to the uncertainty and the long time frames in the Act. It also shows that of the
businesses that identified the Resource Manage ment Act as a constraint, 87 percent of
these were small and medium enterprises,  showing that it is our mum and dad
17 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9433
companies that bear the brunt of these pr oblems. More than half of the cancelled
projects were cancelled in the pre-applica tion stage or well before even receiving a
decision.

items.speaker: Aaron Gilmore
items.text: Why should we be concerned about the impact of the Resource
Management Act on investment?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The uncertainty within the Resource Management Act means
businesses and developers are reluctant to in vest in projects to extend and expand their
operations and are potentially scaling back projects that might otherwise have been
more ambitious. The impacts of this are re al. The delays and uncertainties mean new
jobs are not being created, houses are more  expensive, and communities have no idea
what to expect in their neighbourhoods. Unn ecessary costs are borne by every single
New Zealander in one way or another.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia ora t ātou katoa. Would the Minister
agree with Whanganui iwi that “the voice of  the environment is being overtaken by the
economy” in her Resource Management Act reforms; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: No, I do not agree with that st atement. The greatest gains for
business are very clearly those that come from creating more cer tainty and making the
processes easier to comply w ith. It is not about lowering st andards; it is about having
clearer rules about what you can do and where you can do it. If this House is genuinely
interested in creating jobs and creating opportunities, then I am hopeful that it will back
me in making proposals that make it easie r for new jobs to be created, for new
opportunities to be created, and for New Zealanders to get ahead.

items.speaker: Aaron Gilmore
items.text: How will the Government’s proposed reforms to the Resource
Management Act led by that Minister help to increase investment?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: With a lack of certainty around outcomes and time frames
being a key barrier to investment, we ar e proposing a number of reforms to the
Resource Management Act to address thes e issues—for example, clearer national
guidance, reducing time frames for processi ng consents, and collaborative planning to
create more robust solutions. Providing that sort  of greater certainty will lead to more
jobs and more affordable housing for New Zealanders.
Wanganui Collegiate School—Integration
4. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by his reported statement in relation to Cabinet’s decision to integrate Wanganui
Collegiate, that it was a very difficult decision, but he is sure it was the right thing to do;
if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It is important to note that, at the end of the
day, it was the Minister of Education’s d ecision to integrate Wanganui Collegiate
School, not Cabinet’s. But the Cabinet Manu al is clear that significant statutory
decisions must be discussed at Cabinet. This was a very difficult issue, as the Minister
herself has acknowledged, and Ministers had a range of views on it. We discussed it at
length, after which the Minister of Educati on decided to integrate the school. I do think
that that was the right thing to do, because  Wanganui Collegiate School has been a high
performing school, it has a longs tanding history, the community support for it is very
high in Wanganui, and it plays an important role in the community.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: In 2010 did the Prime Minister have any discussions, including
dinners, with the proprietor, with member s of Wanganui Collegiate School’s Board of
Trustees, or with its lobbyist , Saunders Unsworth, about its intention to apply to
integrate the school; if so, when and with whom?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have those details with  me. I would have to ask my
office. I will put it down in writing if you are prepared to as well.
9434 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Apr 2013

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What instructions or encouragemen t did the Prime Minister give to
the education Minister to start negotiations wi th Wanganui Collegiate School, despite
the advice of ministry officials not to becau se it would be a $3 million a year waste of
money?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: It was a longstanding issue, so I cannot hope to document all
the discussions that took place, but what I ca n say is that the situation was looked at on
its merits. I could see the argument from both sides, but I believe the Minister made the
right decision in integrating the school.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister seek  an update on the proposal to
integrate, as noted by the then education Minister Anne Tolley, on the front of an
August 2010 briefing paper, where she wrote “S end copy of this to PM, please; he has
asked for an update.”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Joined-up Government! The member may well be aware that
the school was in significant financial difficu lty. For a long period of time, when Anne
Tolley was the Minister of Education, there were instances where the Government had
to make a rapid decision as to whether to provide some support to the school to bridge it
while there was a view being taken of whethe r it could integrate it or not. Obviously, I
was interested in what was going on there.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Did the Prime Minister similarl y ask for or request individual
updates on Ōuruhia Model School as it began discus sions on closures last year, or
perhaps Pōtaka School in Gisborne, which is still waiting for news on its future; if not,
why did he single out Wanganui Collegiate School for his very special attention?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In terms of broader schools, there are substantial discussions
that take place between my office—and if yo u want to ask the current Minister of
Education, you know, I have taken an active in terest in what has been happening in
terms of school closures in Christchurch and the impact on those committees. In relation
to Wanganui Collegiate School, I go back to  what I said earlier. The school was in
significant financial difficulty. The Government  was forced to make a decision at the
last minute as to whether it would provide some support for the school. We did that on a
number of occasions, and we did that until a decision could be made about whether the
school would be integrated or not.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Did Cabinet defy the advice of  the education Minister that
integration would be a $3 million a year waste of money, and bail out Wanganui
Collegiate School because the Prime Minister is prepared to bend the rules for elite
schools for wealthy kids?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, we do listen to officials,  and it is no secret that the
Ministry of Education thought we should d ecline the application. The Minister has
considered a wide range of i ssues, and in the end the Mini ster of Education made the
decision to integrate the school.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Will the Prime Minister guarantee that there will be no school
closures or mergers in Wanganui, or citi ng excess capacity within the State school
system; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: That is ultimately a matter for the Minister of Education, not
for me.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to tabl e a 25 August 2010 briefing from the ministry to
the Minister that includes a handwritten note from Minister Anne Tolley, which says:
“Send copy of this to PM, please; he has asked for an update.”

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that briefing. Is there any objection? There
appears to be none.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
17 Apr 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 9435

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I seek leave to table a document dated 4 April 2011, a briefing from
the ministry to the education Minister recommending decline of integration on the basis
of increased State costs and risk of school closures in Wanganui.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is quite a sufficient explana tion. Leave is sought to table that
briefing to the Minister dated 4 April 2011. Is there any objection? There appears to be
none.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Hospitals—Catering Services and Meals on Wheels
5. Hon ANNETTE KING (Labour—Rongotai)  to the Minister of Health : Is he
confident that the Government’s initia tive to provide “Better, Sooner, More
Convenient” health care is meeting his expectations; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Yes, but there is always room for
improvement, and I dare say it is possible we could get an example of that in the next
minute. It is important to understand that, despite tight times, this Government has
invested an extra $2 billion into public hea lth services, including achieving the third-
highest percentage increase of developed nations in the OECD’s latest report.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What is the basis for the claim that he made that more than $10
million per year will be saved through ch anges to hospital food provision, when most
district health boards have made it clear that , like the Prime Minister, they have no clue
how the savings have been estimated, and the Audit Office yesterday reported that
Health Benefits Ltd needs to improve its transparency of reported savings?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: That advice comes from the Health Benefits Ltd information
that has been provided—information that makes it clear that the claim in the House last
week that 50 hospital kitchens would clos e was untrue, and similarly the claim that
1,300 people would lose their jobs was also untrue.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that Meals on Wheels are also included in the
contract, and that the meals ar e to be plated, frozen, and st ored at two production plants
before being transported and stored at a regional distribution hub, then sent to a hospital
kitchen to be reheated, before  being delivered by volunteers to  the clients, and how will
this provision reduce costs and improve quality of food for those who receive it and pay
for it?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I think the member is jumpi ng to assumptions , like she did
last week. What we know is that the proposal at the moment sees 65 percent of the food
cooked on site, which is the complete opposite of what the member told the House only
a week ago.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did he tell the public that the contract to provide hospital
food from two production sites, as set out on  page 33 of the Health Benefits Ltd
document, was “in its early stages”, when Health Benefits Ltd has already shoulder-
tapped the provider, which is already insp ecting hospital kitchens, and staff have
already heard from him last week that “Some people may lose their job,”?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Because clearly it has not even  moved to the formal business
case process for consideration by district heal th boards. Let us be quite frank here: 50
hospital kitchens are not going to close, as Mrs King claims; 1,300 people are not going
to lose their jobs, as Mrs King claimed; and all the food is not being cooked at two
production centres, as Mrs King claimed. I think the biggest apology that needs to come
from this Chamber today is for the fact that Mrs King told so many stories last week.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Talking of stories, when did Health Benefits Ltd advise him that
the contract to provide hospital food from two production sites, wh ich he denied last
week, in a cook-chill style—airline provision of food, with food being able to be kept in
9436 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Apr 2013
the fridge for up to 7 days before being fed to patients—could “lead to negative
publicity that could prove harmful for the Mini ster”, as set out on page 52 of the Health
Benefits Ltd document, if you want a few facts?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I have been kept regularly informed by Health Benefits Ltd of
its activities. I would have to say this to New Zealanders. The No. 1 priority in all of
this is to maintain and improve the quality of food nutrition in New Zealand. That is
why Health Benefits Ltd ha s a group of expert nutritioni sts working with it in
developing this proposal. The public of New Z ealand were misled last week when Mrs
King told them that 50 hospitals would cl ose and 1,300 people would lose their jobs,
and when she said that everything would be served to them frozen. What we know is
that at least two-thirds will be cooked on site . That is quite a different story from what
Mrs King misled them on last week. The N o. 1 priority, though, is  better nutrition for
New Zealanders in hospitals.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a point of order from the Hon Annette King and it
will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table page 58 of  the Health Benefits Ltd report,
showing that all Meals on Wheels will be produc ed in a production plant, and that they
will then go to regional distribution hubs. They will then go to  hospital receiving
kitchens—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! That document has been sufficiently
described to the House. Leave is sought to table page 58. Is there any objection to it
being tabled? There is none. It will be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Heart Disease—Angiograms
6. SCOTT SIMPSON (National—Coromandel)  to the Minister of Health : What
progress is the Government making on im proving access to angiograms for patients
with severe chest pain?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Waiting times for tests and hospital
stays have been reduced for patients in the central North Island with severe chest pain.
Eighteen months ago in the central Nort h Island only a third of the people were
receiving an angiogram at Waikato Hospital within 72 hours of presenting with serious
chest pain—one of the lowest intervention rate s in the country. As a result of a major
project across the five district  health boards, the number of  patients regularly receiving
an angiogram within the 3 days is now over 70 percent.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What measures are Midland district  health boards taking to perform
more angiograms?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The improvement in angiograms and access to better heart
care for patients in the Midland region is a result of a project of  the National Cardiac
Clinical Network and the five Midland di strict health boards. The Midland Acute
Coronary Syndrome project assures that at least 70 percent of patients who have serious
heart symptoms undergo their angiogram within 3 days. Previously, and for many years

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . Today we have seen the Labour Party, eternally in
Opposition, acting exactly like that—eternally  in Opposition. Opportunities have been
given to Labour to start to  act like a Government, but , no, it fails on every single
opportunity.
I want to talk today about something th at should be of importance to all New
Zealanders, and that is the cost of livi ng. Let me begin by acknow ledging first that we
live in the best little country in the world, bar none—bar no ne. This has not come about
by chance, and it certainly has not come about because of any Labour Government that
has ever been in office.
What we should think about is that one of the best things that has happened as a
result of our economic policies has been that interest rates are low. They are around half
of what they were when Labour left office—when it was thrown out in 2008—when our
economy was in recession, when home interest  rates were around 11 percent, and when
the cupboard not only was bare but had been mortgaged as well. Floating interest rates
are now around half of  that—around 5 to 6 percent; around half. For a family with a
$200,000 mortgage—and lots of families around New Zealand have that—that means
$10,000 after tax a year that they get to keep. That is a fantastic achievement, and well
done. And what did we see under Labour? Electricity prices rising by 72 percent.

items.speaker: Hon Tony Ryall
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: By 72 percent. But our economy is growing, benefit
numbers are dropping, crime is down to the lowe st level in 30 years, and we have got a
lot of very strong policies to keep this going.
Actually, today is a very important day because today is, in fact, the funeral of
Baroness Margaret Thatcher. I think everybody  knows that I am a big fan of hers. She
was, however, a person of her time. She was a person of her time. She was influenced
9444 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
by social norms of the day. Looking back, in hindsight, you think that maybe there are a
couple of things she did that  you would not do. But she was always dead right on the
economy and she was always dead right on democracy. She was, as The Economist has
noted this week, a freedom fighter—and she was.
One of the things she said—this is a real ly good quote from her, and I am sure that
the Opposition wants to hear it—goes like this: “Let us ne ver forget this fundamental
truth: the State has no source of money other than money which people earn themselves.
If the State wishes to spend more it can  do so only by borrowing your savings or by
taxing you more. It is no good thinking that someone else will pay—that ‘someone else’
is you. There is no such thing as public m oney; there is only ta xpayers’ money.” Well,
that was true then and it is true today. Of  course, we are working within a budget, and
we have to be very, very car eful about what we do with ot her people’s money. But is it
not great that we can today commemorate the passing of a fantas tic woman, Baroness
Margaret Thatcher?
I would like to celebrate all the other wo men in New Zealand who are doing so well.
That is why I was so pleased to be able to appoint Dr Jackie Blue to the role of Equal
Employment Opportunities Commissioner—very good, Jackie. Jackie Blue would have
to be one of the least partisan MPs in this House—the least partisan. In fact, I have
always said: “See, I have a ppointed a lefty.”, so there you go. Would it not be great in
this Parliament if we coul d have all the women celebrat ing Jackie’s success in her
appointment? Some of you have, and I woul d like to thank all the MPs—male and
female—who have come to support Jackie and to offer her their sincere congratulations.
Jackie Blue is an outstanding New Zeala nder who has spent her life helping others,
helping others in a Parliament that is normally very divisive, and actually trying to bring
people together. She has been chair of thr ee cross-party parliame ntarian groups. All of
them have been around disadvantaged peopl e—women, in particular—and that actually
makes Jackie Blue a fantastic appointment. I am really proud of that, and I have to say
that the country’s gain is the National Party’s loss, Jackie. I am very pleased to have
been able to do that.
I come back to my favourite topic—Barone ss Margaret Thatcher. Let us think about
a few more quotes for the Opposition members,  because they are not very well read.

back and improving the intellectual capacity  of the National Party. Up and down the

had with Baroness Thatcher—not intellect, not  forcefulness, and not leadership, but
accoutrements such as handbags.
I want to turn to the Prime Minister , who is not unlike “The Fisherman of
Parliament”. Like “The Fisherman of Par liament” he does not focus. Most fishermen
focus on whoppers, but when he tells one he pr etends that it is a tiddler—a small lie, a
small untruth. But, in actual fact, up and down the country, in families, marae, and
businesses, they know that this person, this Prime Minister, can no longer be trusted. It
is an arcane area when you ta lk about spies, police agencies, etc. But when you
consistently stand up in th is House and your body language gives it away, and your
colleagues are starting to look down—even if  it does cause my Ra dio Live colleague
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9445
Judith Collins to look up, believing perhaps th at she is the Baroness Thatcher of 2014.
When you see that person looking down, fudging, cannot find the exact words, you
know the poll results in thei r own data collection are going only one way. They are
going the way—not only down but also, as Paul Quinn rises, their fortunes slip. It could
be that that is the final feature they have to offer, given the poor performance.
It is not unreasonable that the Prime Mi nister should take a delegation and be
patriotic in Asia to drum up business, but do not go there and declare war on North
Korea. It is not unreasonable that the Pr ime Minister would want to shoulder-tap
someone whom he may think is a reasonable applicant for a very important position, but
do not come to this House and hide that. Do  not come to this House and conceal that,
and then get panicked into making a half -baked admission, and then go overseas and
pretend that neither he nor Steven Joyce knew anything about the leaks. Those are not
the hallmarks of a Prime Minister.
But, anyway, we have heard up and down th e country the promise that the sale of
these assets is going to improve the economy, that energy prices will become less of a
burden, and that jobs will flow. I can tell  you that up and down the country people
loathe the idea of paying higher prices for pow er. People loathe the idea that foreigners
are going to end up owning more of our assets as a direct consequence of that side of
the House. Those members want only one th ing. They want to hock off these assets,
reward a narrow caste of their fellow travelle rs, and they do not give a hoot about the
long-suffering, garden-variety Kiwis who ca nnot afford property in Auckland, cannot
meet escalating medical-related costs, and cannot find jobs.
In the forestry sector 1 8,000 jobs are at stake—18,000 jobs  are about to dwindle.
This Minister for the Environment, for ex ample, boasts that th e Resource Management
Act reforms are going to deliver new opportuni ty. For 4 years, as a small example, the
forestry sector has been waiting for an environmental policy statement to simplify the
functioning of the forestry sector. Not a di cky-bird. Mills and ma nufacturing plants up
and down the country will applaud the announcement that energy costs are going to
come down, because they are getting no lead ership, no assistance—no assistance from
this Government.
If people do not like those re forms, then they are going to have an opportunity to
give their views. It is called an election. Th at is one reform wher e support will come
massively our way, because there is not a si ngle idea that is lessening the burden of
daily life on Kiwis, and certain ly not from this Prime Minist er, who is a stranger to the
truth.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Tēnā koutou huri noa i t ō tātou
Whare. I am delighted to stand and speak on this Government’s record in terms of its
contribution to lowering the cost of livi ng. Under that previous administration
electricity went up 8 percent in every year, and let us remember here that those were
great years, when surpluses were being re turned, and yet that same Government was
raking off costs from ordinary New Zealande rs, those whom the previous speaker, the
Hon Shane Jones, and that administration pretended to support. This Government,
however, understands how to both focus on keeping the costs of living down by keeping
interests rates as low as possi ble, by working to get a competitive electricity market by
ensuring that consumers have in their own hands the ability to switch between power
companies, and on the other side of it focus on encouraging work and employment.
First of all, this side of the House understands that it is not Governments that create
wealth; it is businesses, it is employers, and it is ordinary Kiwis who back themselves.
The other side of the House specialises in  slicing and dicing a nd redistributing other
people’s money. Our side of the House special ises in asking how we support businesses
to grow opportunity and grow employment. Ho w do we ensure that more tax stays in
9446 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
the pockets of New Zealanders? Because we believe, actually, that they make better
choices for themselves than Governments do.
On this side of the House we understand that we need to get the best value out of
assets. I, as Minister of Education, am ha ppily awaiting the possibi lities that will flow
from realising value out of our assets. This side of the House understands the distinction
between ownership and shareholding. That side of the House doe s not. We want to
grow the value of our assets. We want to reduce the cost on New Zealanders. We want
to invest and entrust their ability to employ people, to grow the wealth, and to distribute
it. That side of the House does not unders tand that equation. We  understand that it
requires a whole lot of levers . That is why we are having  welfare reform, which, again,
follows the principle and theme of investi ng in what people can do, not what they
cannot do, and in perpetuating independe nce, not dependence—two significant
differences between this side of the House and that side of the House.
We want to invest in education because it has the medium to long term ability to
grow the economy and grow productivity, beca use we believe in New Zealanders who
have skills. We believe that if they have sk ills and they can read and write, then they
can get jobs, they can keep jobs, and they can  grow in those possibi lities. That side of
the House wants people angry and aggrie ved and dependent on it. We do not. We
believe in New Zealanders. We believe in this  country. It is the li ttle country that can
under this Government. Under that Government it is the little country that cannot.
That side of the House and all its friends believe that the answer is to borrow and
pray. Our side of the House believes in the fa ct that we need to pay our debt, get it out
of the way, and support our economy so th at New Zealanders can make choices for
themselves and afford to pay for them. We ha ve done that in some of the toughest years
this country has ever faced. Again, we unders tand, appreciate, and respect that wealth
comes from businesses, from people worki ng, and from releasing value from assets,
which is something we share—pickin g up from my colleague’s earlier
acknowledgments—with Baroness Thatcher. Sh e came into a country in as parlous a
state as we came into in this Government. She recognised that she had to break the hold
of those Opposition members who wanted to keep  the greatness of that country and that
empire down. We here on the other side of the world empathise with that, and
appreciate how important it is to do away with the constraints and the obstacles that
otherwise would prohibit the flow of the creative and imaginat ive genes that New
Zealanders have. That is why we are invest ing in science and innovation. That is why
we are reducing compliance costs. That is wh y we have a Minister  of Health who is
investing in New Zealanders being strong, in  good state, well, and able to look after
themselves, not dependent, aggrieved, and operating on myth, rumour, and half-truths.
Our Government believes in strong Ne w Zealanders, capable of looking after
themselves, not dependent on a bunch of—I see I am being waved to sit down. But can I
say that it is a delight to be on this side of the House with right-thinking New
Zealanders who trust and believe in Kiwis—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: The Ministry for Primary Industries was
informed last October that milk was contaminated with dicyandiamide. What did it do
with that information? Did it inform all othe r milk processors immediately? No, it did
not—no, it did not. Fonterra and the Ministry for Primary In dustries sat on it. They sat
on it right through for another 3 months into 2013 before they let the community know,
before they let their trading partners know, and before they let the other processors,
which were just as likely to be affected by contamination of milk by dicyandiamide,
know. So what was this? This  was basically a major c over-up, a damage control
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9447
operation, by part of the industry, but not by a ll of those in the industry. They could not
even participate, as they were not told.
The Official Information Act papers that the Green Party has obtained show that the
team working on this issue was almost singul arly focused on not letting the story get
out. What was its concern? Well, it had quotes like that it was agre ed that “until the
meeting on 21 [January with Fonterra] the issue will stay between the two parties
without involving other organisations.” and th at “MPI need to be careful of the time
frame between being made aware of the issue and communicating this to the public …”.
This is a public that could buy something th at may or may not have been contaminated.
There are obviously a range of views on th e risks to that public. The ministry had
contingencies for when the balloon went up. It  had words like the run-up to “D-Day”,
and said: “Ideally we would like no media coverage.”
Our regulators should be concerned with food safe ty, producing high-quality
products, and protecting our in ternational reputation, which needs to be maintained.
Clearly, that was part of that, but was that th e right way to go about  it? It certainly was
not. Not keeping food contamination a secret, being open, and letting people know what
was going on straight away would have been  a good idea. I am sure there have been
lessons learnt, but it was 3 months later before they made it public. Not only that,
Fonterra has also got a lot to answer for,  because it had the results from August 2012.
The ministry decided to tell the world it was September, but it actually had them earlier.
The results were coming through on 24 August, 27 August—it did know that back then.
But there was another issue in behind there. In the meantime, while this was all
happening, the Fonterra share float happene d. Of course, while that happened—and a
number of people in here will have been at Darfield on 30 Nove mber, opening the big
new factory, when the share float effec tively happened—it went up by 20 percent in
value in the first few minutes. But all that  time it was sitting on the fact that it had
something that it knew would affect markets and would aff ect the reaction of people to
that share float. Exporters re ported very, very qu ickly that sales fell through the floor
after the news broke.
Is there an alternative?  Of course there is an alternative. We do not need to be using
theoretical silver bullets that will bite us in the butt, because th ey are a short-lived,
unsustainable solution to an unsustainable  farming system. There are good solutions.
The solutions are in using sustainable farm ing systems—genuinely sustainable farming
systems—that tick all the boxes. They ensure  farm profitability, like organics can do,
and does, when it is given the opportunity in this country and is not suppressed by the
Government or by the principal people in the sector. Clean, sa fe food is possible in this
country and, as I say, it is profitable, as well. The demand for organics, for example, has
just gone up, by 28 percent in 2012—30 percent up in prices, as well.
I note that the ministry, when it has ever  looked for dicyandiamide—even when it
tested for itself further back, in 2010—did not even do it properly. It looked when there
was a narrow window when it would not be found, and it was in areas where it would
not be found. We can do better, and organics is part of it.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am sad to say that this is a sad day in this
House. It is a sad day for a couple of reasons . The very first reason is that one of the
first speakers from the Opposition, in 2013, when speaking about women politicians—
fine women leaders in this House—reduced  the conversation to being about handbags.
Not one—not one—female member of the Opposition took umbrage at that neanderthal,
sexist language that was displayed by that memb er. I have to say that I am sad to be in
this House in 2013, with the soon to be  starting Equal Employment Opportunities
Commissioner, Dr Jackie Blue, and have that kind of statem ent said in this House and
accepted by those female Opposition members. I am sorry, and it is a sad day in this
9448 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
House when we tolerate that kind of sexist  language, that neanderthal language, when
we have strong, competent, fine women represented across this House.
It is particularly sad because of the timing of today—today, of course, being the
funeral for Baroness Thatcher.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Trivial matters! Talk about the real issues.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: “Talk about the real issues.” , bellows one member from the
other side of the House. Talk about the real issues? What did we cover today in question
time? Yes, the real issues that matter for New Zealanders. The real issues that matter for
New Zealanders are low interest rates,  reducing crime, increasing early childhood
education participation, increasing result s in National Certificate of Educational
Achievement (NCEA) level 2, decreasing numbers on benefits , and growing the
economy. Those actually are the things that matter to New Zealanders.
I want to come back to this connection with Baroness Thatcher. She took office in
very, very challenging times. She took offi ce when the economy from the previous
Government was in a shocking, shocking state.  She was not liked by all, but she did an
incredible job with difficult environments, and she got results. That is what this side of
the House, that is what this Government, is  doing in every area that I mentioned before.
Those are the results, those are the things that matter to hard-working, taxpaying New
Zealanders, not some of the personal, petty, sexist politics that we had today from a
member of the Labour Party.
I am proud to be part of a caucus where we have fine female Mi nisters in Cabinet.
We have had two today who have already spoken  about the results that this side of the
House is producing. The fact is that we  have a very fine Equal Employment
Opportunities Commissioner in Dr Jackie Blue, effective fr om next month. I am proud
of the results that our Government produces . I am proud of our woman MPs. I am not
afraid to stand in this Hous e and be proud of the results th at we are producing, because
they are the results that matter to New Zealanders.
I want to come back to the conversation about the cost of living. Price increases
clearly make it difficult for households. So  in the House today the Labour Opposition
raised questions about power prices. How ironi c is that! Under its 9 years, power prices
went up 72 percent. Now it talks about how we must do something about power prices.
Well, actually, this is a Gove rnment that gets stuff done. This is a Government that is
actually doing things that matter for New Z ealanders in terms of keeping prices
manageable.
Looking at an increase in wages—that is an other thing that I did not mention in my
results, but New Zealanders have had gro ss wages increase by 14 percent. That is a
significant number. I want to come back to  the results in NCEA level 2, because we
know that if we want our young people to leave school, get a qua lification, and get a
job, NCEA level 2 is the minimum that they  need. Since we came into office—listen to
this percentage—in 2008, there has been a 6.7 percent increase. That is 6.7 percent. You
guys do not like facts and figures. You do not li ke hearing the facts about what we are
achieving. You do not like the fact that we ar e in tune with what New Zealanders are
interested in, because that side of the House focuses on petty issues—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Apparently you do not
like a lot of things, according to the speaker on her feet. She should be told, because she
has been around for a little bit of time now, to follow the Standing Orders and refer to
the House but not you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I appreciate the member’s comment. The member is quite right, and
the speaker Louise Upston should not bring the Speaker into the debate.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: That side of the House cannot cope with the f act that this
Government is delivering results. The fact that we just had an interruption there means
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9449
that the Opposition does not like the facts and figures, the results that this Government
is producing for hard-working New Zealanders.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I would have a great deal more respect for that
member who just resumed her seat, Louise  Upston, and her views on the representation
of women in this House if she was not standing by while her Government reduced the
equal representation of women on State sector boards—that target—if she did not stand
by while her Government voted against paid pa rental leave, and if she did not stand by
while her Government reduced the training ince ntive allowance for sole parents. If she
actually stood up for women in this House when it mattered, with her vote, I would
have a great deal more confidence and re spect for what she ha s to say about how
women are represented in Parliament.
But let us move on to the real issues, not  about Maggie Thatcher, at all, because
those are not the real issues that New Z ealanders are thinking about. What they are
thinking about is the cost of living. What they know now as a resu lt of this week in
Parliament is that the Prime Minister, John Key,  is clueless. They used to think that he
was just gormless but now they  know he is absolutely cl ueless, because he said so
himself.
Today we learnt—if people did not know this  before—that what Hekia Parata said
before is completely wrong. Just 10 minutes  ago in this House Hekia Parata stood up
and said that the Government wants to keep money in people’s pockets because it thinks
they know best. However, we know that the Government clearly has its hands in
people’s pockets, because today we heard that the petrol tax is going up to the tune of
$20 billion more than the Government needs fo r the roading that it has planned. That is
$20 billion that is coming out  of the pockets of New Z ealand parents, New Zealand
families, which they could be spending on other things, because that Government made
a decision to put the tax up for no real reason at all.
I want to remind New Zealanders that from 1 April this ye ar they are paying more in
ACC levies than they ought to be paying. Even by the officials’ own estimates—the
estimates from Treasury—this Government is taking up to $2 billion each year out of
the pockets of hard-working employees and employers in New Zealand for no other
reason than it can. That money cannot be spent on anything else but injuries and
accidents, because it is an ACC levy. The offici als have told us that the Government is
taking more than $2 billion more than it needs to cover injuries and accidents. That will
sit in surplus in an A CC account, not going anywhere, not doing anything productive,
just simply sitting there creating a surplus in an attempt to make it look as though the
Government’s whole Crown operating expenses  are going into surplus. Well, it is a
nonsense. It is a cruel trick being played by that Government on every worker and every
employer, who are paying more in ACC levies than they need to to cover the costs of
injuries and accidents.

items.speaker: The question needs to be asked
items.text: why is th e Government doing this? It is doing this
because it promised to bring the books back into surplus, and the only way it is able to
do that—because it is not growing the econo my, it is not getting jobs, and it is not
actually bringing productivity into  this country—was to unfai rly go into the pockets of
workers and employers and take more out in ACC levies than what it actually needs.
Today we learnt that that Government’s  decision to actua lly reduce funding for
pharmaceuticals and put prescription costs up ha s increased the cost of pharmaceuticals
by 9.3 percent.
So that is what is driving the cost of liv ing. It is not anything to do with a robust,
burgeoning economy; it is to do with decisions made by that Government quite
deliberately to take money in petrol taxes that it does not need, to take money in ACC
levies that it does not need for accidents and injuries, and to actually make sure that
9450 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
New Zealanders are paying more for their prescription charges. Those are the things that
are creating real stresses on New Zealand families, because they cannot afford to be
propping up that Government’s commitments that it made in order to go into surplus.
When the Government made that commitment, New Zealanders honestly believed that it
was talking about actually getting the economy going. New Zealanders honestly
believed that it was going to go into surplus by getting out of recession. But no. It is
getting into that surplus surreptitiously by ra ising levies, raising taxes, and raising the
cost of living for every New Zealander.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: It is great to be speaking
today with the other women MPs for the National Party. The inspiration for this all-
women debate is the funeral today of Barone ss Margaret Thatcher because, love her or
hate her—and there are many in both cam ps—she was a powerful and determined
woman and she crashed through the glass ceiling of UK politics.
Internationally New Zealanders have been given credit for leading the empowerment
of women, but even so, it ha s been a slow and imperfect process. In 1893 New Zealand
was the first country to give women the vot e and that was a fantastic achievement of
Kate Sheppard from Christchurch and her supporters. But it took until 1919 for an Act
to be passed to allow women to stand for Parliament, and until 1933 before the first
woman MP, Elizabeth McCombs, was elected, and she was elected because her husband
died in office.
It was the mid-1980s before the number of women MPs reached double figures, but
with MMP we went from 20 to 30 percent of  women members, but there has been little
change ever since. In 1997 we got the first female Prim e Minister, the Rt Hon Dame
Jenny Shipley, and then a second one, and then  a series of female appointments that
included the Speaker of the House, the Chief Justice, and the Governor-General. At one
stage all four senior appoi ntments were held by wome n. Now there is only one. But
thanks to those who have gone before, the doo r is open and that is the way it should
be—not quotas, not pedantic balancing, but an absolutely open process for selecting the
best person for the job.
If New Zealand wants to grow the economy, protect our environment, and increase
our quality of life for the next generation, we  need to make sure that the talents and
skills of women are fully understood and used, and we need to appreciate more of what
women can offer, not just the narrow skill set that is generally recognised and utilised.
Margaret Thatcher may have been the firs t and only woman Prime Minister of the UK,
but she got that position through stubborn aggressiveness and basically out-manning the
men.
Often it is a crisis that provides oppor tunities for women. Du ring the Second World
War women ran our businesses, they ran our fa rms, and in many cases record results,
bumper crops, and top returns were deliver ed. During the earthquakes in Christchurch,
in the media we saw men in uniforms, in fl uorescent vests and hard hats, and that was
good, but everywhere women, less visibly, were  also doing the hard yards, doing the
invaluable work, long-term planning, or ganising, supporting, making things happen,
creating new solutions, advocating for the co mmunity, and making sure that everyone
was being looked after.
To hear their stories and recognise thei r achievements, I organised a series of
meetings, called Bird’s Eye View, and it ha s been both fascinating and inspiring. We
have heard from Mary Devine from Ba llantynes, who was instrumental in the
Re:START Mall; from Di Lucas about the Christchurch “black map”, which shows how
it affected our geotechnical information; and from Karen Gilliland about how midwives
kept delivering during the disaster and about how they have rebuilt a better and stronger
headquarters. We have been fascinated by the work of Coralie Winn, Gap Filler, the
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9451
Ministry of Awesome, and much, much mo re. And every week I see new recovery
stories led by women that are worth telling.
So, as we rebuild in Christchurch and as ou r country strives for a brighter future, we
must be smart enough, we must be bold e nough, to appreciate a nd utilise the human
capital of all our citizens—all our citizens—men and women.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I met Maggie Thatcher. She
was beautiful, focused, intelligent, and she could seriously speak—and there the
contrast ends.
This is where we are at with the electric ity-generating sector in New Zealand. Under
a system that National set up and Labour gove rned with, power companies are making
record profits and the Gove rnment is extracting massi ve dividends from power
companies, which is, seriously, an undeclar ed taxation system. We pay tax on petrol,
alcohol, and cigarettes, and the tax is acknowledged. The Government takes hundreds of
millions out of the electricity sector by way of dividends, and the tax is by stealth.
The entire electricity generation sector is a shambles. It is a phoney, fictional market.
The so-called competition is a fantasy designe d to hide what is actually happening. The
model is hopelessly flawed and needs to be radically overhauled—and now. I seriously
doubt there is any person in this country, even someone with a PhD in advanced
electronics or economics, who could give a cl ear, coherent explanation of how the New
Zealand electricity sister—the New Zealand electricity sector—actually functions.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: The “electricity sister”—ha, ha!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, I know that woman over there could not—the
woman who is laughing about it. Apparently , rocketing prices on the farms of her
electorate and in the homes of her part of the country are of no matter, whatsoever. They
are a laughing matter—what is her name?

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Jacqui Dean.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Jacqui Dean does not give a tinker’s damn about a
huge cost to New Zealand businesses, farms,  and homes. Jacqui Dean needs to get out
there and find out what is going on in her electorate.
If one sets out to design a system that would gouge the public with electricity price
hikes, one would create the system we have ended up w ith now. It is a complete
mishmash of half-baked economic theories , foisted on the count ry by National, and
Jacqui Dean thinks it is a great idea. Jacqui Dean does not give a hoot for her electorate.
She thinks this cost structure, which benefits the few—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Where’s that member’s electorate?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is no use hysterically shouting like a fishwife.

items.speaker: Answer the challenge
items.text: what on earth is going on? It is a mess. The public and
businesses are paying through the nose for this mess.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Say my name—say my name.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: No strident, hysterical, anti-feminine call from there
is going to change my mind. The Governme nt ploughs blindly on with its State asset
sales, and the cannon fodder that Jacqui Dean  and her ilk represent just signs up every
day. Something has to be done to earn the “Max Bradford market matters”—remember
what he said? He said: “I’m going to plateau prices.” It was 1998. Well, under National,
this is what electricity plateaus mean. It is  a vertical line, straight up, straight through
the roof, and Mr Key has the audacity to blame Labour for the system that he and his
party set up.
What is the Government doing to reduce electricity prices? Nothing. Despite—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: Turn the lights off—that’s New Zealand First policy, eh?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, I see. The solution th at Tau Henare and Jacqui
Dean have got is that if you want to save el ectricity, turn the lights off. Turn the fridge
9452 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
off. Turn the heater off. In fact, why not ju st turn things off completely? That is their
solution.
I know that there are people from the Pacifi c Islands here, and they will be shocked
to think that this Parliament in the First World has got such puerile debate from one side
of the House, namely the side of the Hous e that is the Government. There, those ones—
not over here. We have predictably been told by Dr Geoff Bertram from Victoria
University that in comparison with the US, the UK, Japan, France, and South Korea, for
example, our prices are much higher.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What are you going to do about it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: What are we going to do  about it? Here is the
answer. This is what our policy is, and today I am announcing it. New Zealand First will
restore the State-owned elect ricity generators now bei ng sold back into public
ownership and put them under a single genera ting entity. We will seriously investigate
putting a cap on electricity pricing related to the CPI, and no more.
Mr Henare said, in a lucid moment: “What is your policy?”. He has heard it. It is
definitive. And, if he concerns himself about  his people up there in west Auckland, he
should be cheering from the rafters that, finally, there was announced today a solution
that will work. We are going to—

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: He’s going to nationalise it—that’s all he could come up with.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, the volume of noise over there suggests that he
should wind up—you are right, Mr Speaker. So  today we have announced our policy,
and tomorrow and in the next few months—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It is ironic is, is it not, that Helen Kelly, Sue
Moroney, and others are so ready to discrimina te against the appointment to the role of
Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner of Dr Jackie Blue, just because she is a
soon-to-be former member of Parliament a nd member of a political party. Should that
disqualify her from being able to step aside from party politics and assume a neutral
role? Do these same women hold that vi ew about, maybe, H V Ross Robertson, who
leaves his Opposition party bench to sit in  the Speaker’s Chair and preside over
Parliament? Well, he can do it, he can be neutral, but Jackie  Blue cannot? Eric Roy can
do it, he can be neutral, but Jackie Blue cannot? Lindsay Tisch can do it, he can be
neutral, but Jackie Blue ca nnot? And what about Helen Clar k? Under those same rules,
is she, therefore, unable to hold a neut ral position at the United Nations? Do these
people even think these things through?
But it is quite different for them, of cour se, is it not, because when Labour was in
power, there were many, many appointments of Labour luvvies. Does anyone remember
Dianne Yates? Lovely woman—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No!

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: No, they said from the other side—no, they said from the other
side. Not even her Labour mates remember  her. Does anyone remember Dame Ann
Hercus? Does anyone remember Mike Williams? Does anyone remember Helen Kelly?
How convenient for them now to discredit J ackie Blue’s years of cross-party work—
those 8 years in Parliament of cross-party wo rk on a number of issues, three or four I
think, including her advocacy of women—he r very, very clear advocacy of women—
and her strong, unforgettable, and successful  campaign for the funding of Herceptin.
What a triumph that was for Jackie Blue—something to be so very proud of. And where
were the Labour women, where were the Green women in 2005, and where were the
New Zealand First women—were there any in 2005? There might have been. Where
were they in 2005 when Jackie Blue was calling on the then Labour Government to help
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9453
save the lives of breast cancer sufferers with the funding of Herceptin? Where were
they? They were silent.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: We funded Herceptin.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Oh, they are talking now. They ar e talking the talk now, but they
were silent when it really mattered. In term s of making a contributi on, Dr Jackie Blue
has done more in this House than most. So, Helen Kelly, Sue Moroney, Metiria Turei—
it is so easy, is it not, to pull someone dow n, to denigrate their work, and to doubt their
motives, just because they do not come from yo ur side of the political spectrum. Well, I
say thank goodness for strong women at any time in history—RIP Maggie Thatcher—in
any Parliament, whether it is in the Un ited Kingdom, it might be in the Pacific
parliaments, or here in New Zealand, w ho are prepared to have a view, who are
prepared to stand up for what matters to them, and who, like Dr Jackie Blue, want to act
in a role to provide equal opportunities for all of us.
This week we welcome parliamentaria ns from all around the Pacific to our
Parliament. This is the first time such a significant number of Pacific MPs and political
leaders have assembled together to discuss the key issues facing the Pacific region. The
forum is a good opportunity for us to develo p networks with our Pacific colleagues.
Although many Pacific Island countries have  a pool of well-educated women who are
already leaders in their fields, women’s partic ipation in these parlia ments varies from a
high of 44 percent—not so bad—to three countries who have no women
parliamentarians. Would it not be great to  encourage and assist women to conduct
successful election campaigns and to become effective MPs? We need strong women in
all of our parliaments, so let us celebrate and encourage and not try to pull each other
down, just for the hell of it. Thank you.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: When the Government set up the
Auckland super-city many people said it would have very far-reaching consequences,
and there is no doubt that right now Auckland is on the move. For the first time ever the
city has a plan to deal with growth, it is dealing with the gridlock, Wynyard Quarter and
Britomart Place have shown what high-quality urban renewal can do, and the place is
really buzzing. There is a new sense of unity and pride in Auckland.
Unfortunately, there is one thing holding it back like a dead weight—Wellington.
Although Auckland is moving fast to tran sform its regional economy to focus on
innovation and exports, the National Government  is a brake on progress. But when it
comes to the big issues in Auckland, the G overnment has no plan of its own. All it
knows how to say is no to Auckland, no to the popular city rail link that would have
allowed trains to run every 5 minutes and th at is supported by more than 60 percent of
Aucklanders, and no to the Auckland Unitary Plan that would allow Auckland to grow a
little bit up and a little bit out.
And what has the Government done? It ha s dispatched Laurel and Hardy—big Gerry
Brownlee, the tsar of Christchurch, and Nick Smith, the MP for Nelson; Nick Smith, the
“Minister for Sprawl”, and Gerry Brownlee, the “Minister for Gridlock”—to tell
Aucklanders how to run their city. Well, I ha ve got a word of warning for the National

items.speaker: Government
items.text: Aucklanders are getting fe d up with Laurel and Hardy coming to
Auckland and telling them how to run their city. Aucklanders had the super-city forced
on to them. They accepted it, they are maki ng it work, but Wellington simply cannot let
go, because their man John Banks did not win the mayoralty.
While Gerry Brownlee pours scorn on the city  rail link and Nick Smith threatens to
legislate to take powers away from the Auckla nd Council, the Prime Minister is all over
the place. In recent weeks we have seen  him misleading Aucklanders, misleading the
public, on two key issues. He said that the Auckland Council wants the Government to
enact the unitary plan  straight away with no input a nd no opportunity for Aucklanders
9454 General Debate 17 Apr 2013
to have a say. Wrong. Right now thousands of  Aucklanders are having their say, and,
once the plan is notified in September, even if the Government gives it legal weight like
the council has asked, the public can do it  all again with the Government-appointed
independent panel. How is that for ha ving no input? Why is the Prime Minister
misleading the public?
He was caught out again when he said on te levision that Auckland Council is saying
it is going to intensify, it is  pretty much going to go up within the urban metropolitan
limits—just go straight up—and we are sayi ng you need to go up and out. Nothing
could be more misleading. The Auckland Pl an says that up to  40 percent of new
dwellings will be buil t on greenfields land over the next  30 years. For the benefit of
Nick Smith, what that means is that land equivalent to six times the area of Nelson will
be freed up outside the current urban boundaries.
It is a shame that the Prime Minister does not agree with Kim Campbell of the
Employers and Manufacturers Association, w ho said recently that the Government’s
refusal to ratify Auckland’s plan before 2016- 17 will load big costs on to Auckland’s
ratepayers and hold back Auckland’s growth. It  is a shame that he does not agree with
John Roughan of the New Zealand Herald , who said that the Government is “on the
wrong side of the city’s plan” and that no one else is putting up an alternative. It is a
shame that the Prime Minister does not agr ee with Federated Farmers Chief Executive,
Conor English, who says that Auckland need s to stop sprawling across the countryside
and invest more in public transport. That  sounds remarkably close to Len Brown’s
Auckland Plan. So not only is the Govern ment offside with Aucklanders but the
National Party’s closest political allies in Auckland—the Employers and Manufacturers
Association, Federated Farmers, and the ch amber of commerce—have all deserted the
National Party and are backing Len Brown’s vision for Auckland.
Labour’s policy is to back Aucklanders, not to fight them. We agree with the
Auckland Council, we agree with its balanced  approach to managing the city’s growth
and the fact that our country’s biggest city has to incorporate a million extra people in
the next 30 years, and we agree with th e balanced approach to land supply and
intensification. Labour will invest in the city rail link, because it will allow trains to run
on our rail network every 5 minutes. The bigge st roadblock to progress in Auckland is
this Government, and New Zealanders deserve better.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak in this general debate,
which is more than likely going to be my fina l general debate. I would like to begin by
acknowledging the many, many MPs in the House who have wished me well in my new
role as the Equal Employment Opportunitie s Commissioner, which I begin in early
June. I want to acknowledge the contri bution that the former Equal Employment
Opportunities Commissioner, Dr Judy McGregor, has made in this role. Her work
output has been extensive and her work extr aordinary and outstanding. I have got huge,
massive shoes to fill, I know, and I will certai nly do my very best to do that. I am truly
and sincerely humbled by the messages of support from throughout the House and also
from well-wishers around the country.
On this day I would like to acknowledge all women MPs in ev ery party in this
House. It is not easy being a woman MP—it ain’ t easy, that is for sure. At times it is
brutal, it is personal, it is combative, and it is host ile. So well done, everyone—all
women MPs in this House. And, with the exception of the Green Party, women MPs are
in the minority in their respective parties. We make up 50 percent of the population, and
it is unacceptable that we make up a little  over 30 percent of th e current Parliament.
That, I know, by international standards is not bad. But New Zealand has been a leader
in this area. We gave women suffrage in 1893; we can do it ag ain. I lay down that
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9455
challenge to all parties, with the exception of the Green Party, and that is also for future
political parties that might be forming.
I would like to particularly acknowledge the cross-party groups th at I have had the
pleasure to work in over the last 7 years.  They are the New Zealand Parliamentarians’
Group on Population and Development, and that role has a focus on sexual reproductive
health and rights of women in  Pacific Island countries, dom estic violence, and our aid
budget; and the Commonwealth Women Parliame ntarians group, which I co-chair with
Louisa Wall, which has the focus of incr easing the number of wo men MPs in Pacific
parliaments. That is why we  are so very excited about the Pacific forum tomorrow and
the debate that it will have about gender. We are looking forward to that very much.
I have so much enjoyed working in the cross-party space, working collectively for an
objective with like-minded people. Whether it is about sexual reproductive health and
rights or increasing the number  of women MPs in Pacific pa rliaments or whether it is
lobbying for the Arms Trade Treaty, it has been  a pure pleasure, it has been rewarding,
and I have enjoyed it immensely.
The work, particularly in the New Zeal and Parliamentarians’ Group on Population
and Development, has left me with the abso lute and utter conviction and passion that in
developing countries, by backing and empowering women and girls, economies,
countries, and communities will go forwar d. But the same applies to the developed
countries. As women progress, everyone progresses, and that is why I am so thrilled and
excited about my new role.
Judith Collins told the House today that, with my appointment to Equal Employment
Opportunities Commissioner, sh e has appointed a lefty to the position. She said that
with mirth, but I will wear that as a badge of honour.
I am grateful that while I ha ve had the opportunity  to be a member of Parliament in
this House, I have been given the opportunity to advocat e in a number of areas, which I
will just outline as time allows. But, first of all, I would like to wish Louisa Wall really
well in the third reading of her Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill.
I have a bill in the ballot , which I hope a colleague will  take up, and that is the
Marriage (Court Consent to Marriage of Minors) Amendment Bill. That bill would
mean that if young people of 16 or 17 wish to  get married, they will need to go through
the Family Court. Parental consent is  out of the loop, though, obviously, when the
Family Court judge hears an  application, the family w ould be included. I believe
sincerely that that would take possible coerci on out as a factor with the marriages of
young people. These marriages happen only about 100 times a year, so in the
background of 20,000-plus marriages each year, we are talking about a small number.
So I am hopeful that a colleague will take th at up and that it will get drawn, be debated,
and pass through the House.
I am particularly proud, and I will always be  proud, of the fact that the Government
took up the 12 months’ funding of Herceptin—absolutely. I know that has made—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Jackie, it was your work, too.

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: Well, yes, it has made an e normous difference. Studies that
have since come through have proved be yond any shadow of doubt that 12 months is
the gold standard. I am so proud a Nationa l Government funded it immediately after
becoming the Government in 2008.
I am also particularly pleased that I have had the opportunity to advocate for enrolled
nurses, and I am pleased that the Minister of Health expanded that role into acute
services, as well.
Mr Speaker, thank you for your leadership in the House. Thank you, everyone, each
and all, thank you so much.
9456 General Debate 17 Apr 2013

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Kia
ora tātau katoa. I a au e tū nei me mihi rā ki tērā mema i tū ki mua i te aroaro o te Whare
