Pāremata i tēnei ahiahi i a ia e kōrero ana mō ngā mea kua oti i a ia.
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker, and to us all. As I stand here I must acknowledge that
member who stood before the House of Parliament this afternoon while she was talking
about the things she had done.]
So can I just add my congratulations to Jackie Blue and thank her for her
contribution. I feel a bit of a killjoy after that speech, with all its positivity, in raising the
issue that I want to put before the House. I wish you well, Jackie, in your career ahead
of you.
In the time I have got, I want to talk about a topic that often provokes all sorts of
severe reactions, as if it were the first time  the words have ever been uttered. What I am
talking about is the topic of institutional raci sm. Over 30 years ago it was identified that
Māori experience disproportionate treatment in  the New Zealand justice system. People
do not see things such as overrepresentation of M āori in all of the worst statistics as a
result of racism; on the contrary, th ey tend to think that it is a M āori problem that we
often try to justify by claiming racism. I reje ct that. Those are ignorant and divisive
thoughts, and they are preserved by our cu rrent systems, which are geared towards
disadvantaging M āori in the police force, the courts , corrections, and,  of course, the
justice system.
One of the good things about being in Parliame nt is that you get clear statistics and
information that might back the claim. Of  course, in the past week or so, the
organisation JustSpeak released a very clear  overview that spoke about the chances of
being prosecuted for a crime if you are a young Māori. It said that it was far more likely
that you would be pros ecuted if you were M āori than non-M āori. For the 3,495 theft
apprehensions recorded as Caucasian there were 588 prosecutions, and for M āori, for
the 5,660 apprehensions recorded, 1,173 resulted  in prosecution—in other words, rates
of 16.8 percent versus 20.7 perc ent. Even worse, there ar e 15 categories of offences,
ranging from homicide to theft to property o ffences, with everything in between, and in
14 of those 15 categories M āori have a higher proportion of  apprehensions leading to
prosecutions. The category that is the exception is “miscellaneous offences”.
Such was our concern about this that we as ked questions of the Minister of Police,
who is in the House at present, about this  matter. It is something that we do take
seriously, and we will continue to advocate against this type of racism.
Most people would think th at there is a simple reason—if you commit a crime, then
you do the time. The thing is that following ap prehension for a crime, the percentage of
Māori who are then prosecuted is far higher than the percentage of P ākehā who are
prosecuted. If a M āori teen and a P ākehā teen are apprehended for the same crime, the
young Māori is more likely to be prosecuted, while the P ākehā youth is more likely to
get off. Does this not raise questions of fa irness and of discrimi nation in those people
who would be sceptical of in stitutional racism? That is th e question. Sadly, I would not
expect so.
When the apprehension of a suspect occurs, there is often an element described as
discretion. It can be used by th e arresting officer as to wh ether to proceed or to not
arrest. One might ask what is considered by that officer when they are using their
notions of discretion. Are their decisions going to be informed by their own views about
Māori people and about P ākehā people? Once in the system , of course, what are the
options that are being offered to offenders that might enable  them to plan for a future
without being stigmatised by the slur of  a criminal conviction? We know about
diversion schemes and restor ative justice programmes, but  are those being offered
fairly? Are they being offered to young people, in order that they might be able to avoid
17 Apr 2013 General Debate 9457
conviction and have a shot at growing up and learning from their experiences? The data
that was presented by JustSpeak suggests not.
Ethnic bias within the police and criminal justice system is real. There have been
numerous instances and reports in New Zealand that tell us that it is real. Kim Workman
from the Rethinking Crime and Punishment group suggests that there are a number of
avenues that need to be looked at, includi ng traffic stop procedures, ethnic profiling,
offender eligibility for diversion, and pre-char ge warnings, to name a few. I have been
interested in the whole notion of community law forums. So that is the concern, and the
Māori Party will be raising a bill in the near future called the Elimination of Institutional
Racism Bill, and we hope to introduce that into the members’ ballot very shortly.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
HOLIDAYS (FULL RECOGNITION OF WAITANGI DAY AND ANZAC DAY)
Third Reading
GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central)  on behalf of Dr David

items.speaker: Clark
items.text: I move, That the Holidays (Full Recognition of
Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . As many
colleagues around the House will know, Dr  David Clark is on an Eisenhower
Fellowship in the United States of America. He has asked me to step in and do this third
reading. I am very happy to do so because th is bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition of
Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill, was in the members’ ballot
originally under my name—and there is no trut h to the rumour that  I ordered Dr Clark
away from the building so I could do this. Th is bill is one that was also in Darien
Fenton’s name for a period of time, and I am very pleased that  the Labour caucus’
members who were involved in the original  drafting of the bill  will now have the
opportunity to speak on it.
At the very outset I would like to thank the parties that ha ve supported this bill right
from its first reading—the Green Party, New Zealand First, the M āori Party, Mana,
United Future, and Brendan Horan. The support of  all of those parties and MPs is much
appreciated. All of those parties have taken this bill as a point of principle, and I thank
them very much for sticking to their principles on this issue.
The origins of the bill were in 2010 when  both Anzac Day and Waitangi Day fell on
weekends and there was no holiday on Monda y for either of them. That year, New
Zealanders got only nine of the 11 public ho lidays that they are entitled to under the
Holidays Act. That is not fair, and this bill  seeks to give hard-working New Zealanders
a fair go—time to spend with their families and to continue to commemorate these
important days in our calendar, 7 years out of 7.
We do need to recognise the value of ho lidays to working people and indeed to
businesses. Holidays are about recharging. Th ey are about spending time with families,
about enjoying recreation and downtime. Th ey are actually very important for
productivity, for good morale in the workplace. That is what holidays are for. They are
not things that should be begrudged by the Government; they  are things that should be
supported by the Government.
It is important to note that this bill does recognise the importance and significance of
these 2 days to New Zealanders. Waitangi  Day is our national day, and as David
Shearer and others have stated, we need to continue to work to ensure that it is both a
day of reflection on our past and present and a celebration of what we have and what we
can become. Anzac Day assumes a greater sign ificance every year in our country. It
does note our coming of age as a nation on th e battlefields of World War I, and the
9458 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
sacrifice of New Zealanders then and in other conflicts that have followed. It is a day of
commemoration that we hold dear and that grows in importance every single year.
Next Thursday we will commemorate An zac Day, and thousands and thousands of
New Zealanders around the country will go out to do this at Dawn Services, at
community services, right around the country . That is important. It will also be a
holiday. It will not diminish the day at all, as  it has not done in past years. The same
will now be the case as a result of this bill when the day falls on a Saturday or a Sunday.
Let me be absolutely clear. The commemo rations of Anzac Day and Waitangi Day
will continue to be on 25 April and 6 February  every year, as they should be, but there
will be a holiday every 7 out of 7 years, not just 5 out of 7 years. This is already the way
that things are done in most of the states of Australia—i n Western Australia, Victoria,
ACT, New South Wales, South Australia, Qu eensland, and the Northern Territory. All
of them have—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Do they care about Anzac Day?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right. As my collea gue says: “Do they care about
Anzac Day?”. You bet they do. The reports from Australia, where the Mondayisation
process is in place, indicate that the nu mbers of people attending Anzac Day services
are increasing year on year. It is also wh at we do for Christmas Day and Boxing Day
and New Year’s Day, and ther e is no confusion. If Christ mas Day falls on a Saturday,
the presents are opened, people attend church services, and the only change is that the
day after Boxing Day we get a holiday for it. That is what will happen in this case.
So workers support this bill in large numb ers, but so do many businesses. They
recognise the value of holidays for their worker s. They also know that the cost of this
bill is not huge. It is already dealt with, and budgeted for, by businesses, 5 out of 7
years, and it is simply a matter of making that  7 out of 7 years. In previous calls I have
noted the work that David Farrar, the Nationa l Party’s pollster, has done. He has said
that this represents 0.12 percen t of an annual wage bill. I wa nt to actually congratulate
Mr Farrar. It is a pity he was not able to influence the National Party with his support
for this bill, but employers across the boa rd have been coming forward and supporting
this legislation. I particularly want to acknowledge the Tourism Industry Association,
which has strongly supported th is bill. In its submission to  the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee it said that any costs a ssociated with this bill will be outweighed
by the overall economic benefit. That is  a statement from the Tourism Industry
Association that can be applied right acr oss the board. Real economic benefits will
occur as a result of this legislation.
Unfortunately, with all of the parties that I have mentioned, for whose support we are
grateful, the National Party has yet to come around to supporting this bill. Well, it is not
too late. It is not too late for the National Pa rty to come on board, get on the right side
of history, and get on the right side of the othe r parties in this Parliament. I have got no
hope for John Banks, by the way. I am not aski ng for him to come on board with it, but
there is a chance for the National Party to come on board today and say: “We support
workers. We support workers having the ability to spend more time with their families.”
But the track record does not look good, in terms of bringing them across, because
every time legislation that gives more holid ays to workers comes up in this House, the
National Party opposes it. When the 4 weeks’ annual leave came in, the sky did not fall
in. Nothing happened that went wrong there.  Business productivity and profits went up
after the 4 weeks’ annual l eave came in, but the National Pa rty still opposed it. But it is
not too late. National can come in and say that its commitment to supporting families
actually has some reality, that it is prepared to back a piece of legislation that is going to
make sure that people have more time with their families.
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9459
But the National Party’s criticisms of this  bill have ranged. They have ranged from
the fact that this is the end of civilisation as we know  it, through to: “Why are you
bothering? It doesn’t make any difference.” The National Party needs to get a consistent
stance on that. But in the end, it has the chan ce today to get on to the right side of
history and vote for this le gislation. Many people have as ked when this provision will
next come into effect. The next time that  this will happen is on 25 April 2015, when
Anzac Day will fall on a Saturday, the following year Waitangi Day will fall on a
Saturday, and then in 4 and 5-year gaps after that.
We on this side of the House are not pretendi ng that this is the bi g issue in industrial
relations. We are not saying that . What we are saying is he re is an opportunity to do
something. Here is an opportunity to give  New Zealanders a fa ir go. Here is an
opportunity to give New Zealanders some more  time with their families. It is not the
biggest thing in the world in industrial relations, but it is important. It represents an
important principle—that people deserve to have holidays; that those holidays in the
law, 11 public holidays, should be granted.
We know that there are bigger issues out th ere for workers—the loss of thousands of
jobs, wages not keeping pace with the cost of living, precarious work, and the coming
changes to employment law from this Government. These are all big issues and they are
ones we need to be working on. This bill is not on that scale, but it can do a simple thing
for workers. It can give them a fair go, it can  give them time with their families, and it
continues to ensure that we commemorate thes e important days in our calendar. This is
a fine bill, and I have great pleasure in commending it to the House.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Since Mr Grant Robertson just
gave the opening speech on this bill, th e Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day
and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill, I think we a ll need to pay credit to Dr David Clark
for the work he has done on it. This is act ually his bill. I would not let Mr Robertson
take credit for the bill.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: It was mine.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: He says it was his bill, but no, David Clark is the one who has
promoted this bill. David Clark is the one who has done the work on this bill, and—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: It was his bill first, David.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I know what you are saying, but  Mr Clark is the one who
actually should be promoted he re today, not Mr Robertson. I th ink it is strange that the
Labour Party members are now fighting amongs t themselves over who is to take the
credit for this bill. That is a very disappointing thing, but it just shows the contempt that
Labour Party members hold for their own memb ership—the way that they treat their
colleagues in this House. Today we are seeing a battle between two Labour front-
benchers over who should actually take the credit for this bill when this is a serious bill.
I would like to pay tribut e to the Transport and Indus trial Relations Committee,
which actually looked at this bill and went through all the ar guments in a very fair and
reasonable way. It was very well led, I must admit, through the select committee
consideration, and I think Mr Clark should take  a lot of credit for the way he actually
approached the bill, unlike other members of the Labour Party here today, who are
trying to make mischief while one of their me mbers is out of the country. It is a shame
that they will do that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can I just remind the
member that it is out of or der to refer to someone being absent from the Chamber. All
of us have to take time from the Chamber sometimes.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, I understand that.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How long has he been here?
9460 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Clark? He has been here for just his first term. I think it is
disappointing that you do th at to a first-term member and try to take the credit away
from him—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The member cannot bring
you into debate, and he just did.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: You are absolutely right.
You cannot bring the Speaker into the debate.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Just to the people listening, I say that I think it is disappointing
that we are talking about a se rious bill here and the Labour Pa rty, for the first couple of
minutes of my speech, has been attacking the National Party around who is actually in
control of that bill. I think that is very disappointing, coming from the Labour Party.
When we have a look at this bill, this is a bill where we understand the arguments on
both sides. There are good arguments on both  sides for this bill. Nobody denies the
important role that holidays play in the work ing life of people, to give them the chance
to spend time with their friends and family in the community.
We have very special days in New Z ealand that are represented by holidays.
Traditionally, you have the statutory holiday s, the 11 basic public holidays, which are
very important to our culture and our community. We also have the annual holidays that
are available to New Zealanders, as we ll. If you look at New Zealand, you have 11
public holidays and 20 days’ minimum annual pa id leave. If you go to another country
like, for example, the United States, it has 10 public holidays and it has zero minimum
annual paid leave. So New Zealand has a very generous system, and nobody would hold
that against the New Zealand community or workers or anybody involved in the system.
I think the holidays that we are talking about today, Waitangi Day and Anzac Day, are
especially special days, because they repres ent very strong parts of  our history and our
country going forward, and I think nobody takes that away from those very special
days.
So this is not an attack on workers, as the Labour Party will try to portray—it is far
from that. It is not the situation, as Mr Robe rtson has tried to indicate, that the National
Party does not support workers. That is not th e case. This is a case where the National
Party likes to take into account the full circumstances around this issue.
One of the big circumstances that I think peopl e need to be aware of in this debate is
the actual effect of this bi ll. In 2015 there will be 1 day that will be Mondayised, in
2016 there will be another day, and then ther e will be nothing until 2020. So the effect
of this bill is very remote in the extreme. This is not a big bill that is going to deliver for
New Zealand workers or for the New Zealan d community. This is not a bill of the
consequence that the Labour Party tries to portr ay, and it is a bit sad that it even has to
fight over a bill that does not have that consequence either.
The next time this bill will be effective will be in 2015, and that will be with Anzac
Day, and then in 2016 it will be with Waitangi  Day. Then workers will have to wait
until 2020 for the next Anzac Day.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Well, come on, move an amendment. We’ll give you leave.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: So this bill does not have a lot of effect on New Zealand
workers. What are you saying, Trevor?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Add three or four more—we’ll give leave.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: So Mr Mallard wants to add more days. Well, this bill does not
add more days. It indicates that these days—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That Government’s taking them away.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, we are not taking them awa y. Mr Mallard is saying we are
taking them away; that is just not the case. We have been through this before with Mr
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9461
Mallard about getting the facts right. It is simply not the case th at anything is being
taken away.
In New Zealand we value the role that our public holidays have in our community
and in our country. We understand the impor tance of them. The National Party, by not
voting for this bill, is not attacking workers’ rights. It is merely that we represent that
there are some other issues involved in this bill. For me, one of th e big issues involved
in this bill is that it has limited effect. Wa iting until 2020 to see any effect is not a big
thing. It is a bit like the Labour Party and its superannuation policy. That will not have
any effect until 2025, will it? That was its last superannuation policy. It might be
interesting to see how the new one actually pa ns out. But this bill do es not have a large
effect in the immediate future, and that is a shame for this House.
When we actually went through it in the select committee, there were a number of
submissions in favour of this bill. I would like to thank those submitters for coming in
and for the way that they did their submissi ons. I would like to thank the variety of
submitters we had, as well.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How many did you have?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: We had numerous submissions, and there were a lot of
arguments made around different sorts of issues in the bill. One of the big issues is the
actual cost of the potential holiday. That is something that there was some debate within
the select committee around, that cost.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What was the cost?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Well, because the cost indicate d—there is always a financial
cost, if you are granting a ho liday. But then ther e were arguments made that there is
actually a financial gain too for the potential  spending in such things as the tourism
community and suchlike. Those are valid arguments that were put up. The select
committee considered them at length and came to very good conclusions around them.
This bill is a good start by Mr Clark in his political career. It is a bill that he has
portrayed and built through this House, a nd we commend him for that. Unfortunately,
though, this bill has some issues with it. It doe s not have a large effect in the immediate
future, and that is why it is a bit sad that  the Labour Party is pi nning its hopes on this
bill. There are other ways that we can addr ess these issues. I recommend to the House
that this bill is something that we should c onsider, but, unfortunatel y, at this stage the
National Party will not be voting for this bill.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It is with great pleasure that I speak in the third
reading of the Holidays (Full Recogni tion of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day)
Amendment Bill. My only regret is that its sponsor, Dr David Clark, is not here to see it
pass through this third reading. I want to send my congratulations to him in America, as
I know, indeed, Grant Robertson and all of the Labour caucus do, on the great work he
has done on this member’s bill. I am also acknowledging the role that Grant Robertson
has played, but it has been a Labour effort, actually. We ha ve all worked hard to see
through a change that actually does change life for the better for working people.
It is not often that that happens, and it certainly never happens under a National
Government, so this is a special day. This is a very special day, considering that we
have had 5 years of attacks on workers’ rights. Those attacks have included a foolish
dependence on being able to sack people within 90 days without reasonable justification
as a job creation measure, a minimum wage that has increased by only $5.60 a week, or
just 14c an hour in re al terms, over the 5 years since National became the Government,
and cuts to the wages of young people that come into effect on—guess which day? On 1
May—International Workers’ Day. There is a wonderful reward for young people, the
hard-working young people of the country, on International Workers’ Day, 1 May!
9462 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
There is more to come. We know the legislation is heading our way. The
employment law changes are coming. And—you know what—the Government is even
going to cut workers’ tea and meal breaks. It is even going to make cuts to the tea break,
the smokers’ break—the smoko break. Hard -working New Zealanders have been
forgotten by this Government. It cannot even bring itself to support what it knows in its
heart of hearts is the right thing to do. It is the right thing to do.
We have heard some interesting arguments through the passage of this bill, but one
that has been canvassed at length by the Natio nal Party is that it undermines the special
nature of Anzac Day. Anzac Day, on 25 April,  has been a holiday since 1921. It was
first gazetted as a half-day holiday in 1916. But back then a ho liday meant a real
holiday. It meant a real day off, like Sundays used to be when no shops were open—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Even Saturdays.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: —even Saturdays, that is right —the pubs were shut, the local
dairy was closed, and the buses did not run. That is what it used to be like.
A lot has changed through the last hundred years. There have been several
amendments to the Holidays Act and there ha ve been several amendments to the Anzac
Day Act and the Waitangi Day Act. Annual leave and public ho lidays have been
increased, without the vote of the Nationa l Party, of course—wit hout its support. But
also what has changed is that more workers are now expected to work on public
holidays. So while the pubs and shops are still closed on Anzac Day morning—it is only
until 1 o’clock, whereas once it was the whole day—on Waitangi Day it is a free-for-all,
so everything is open. Meanwhile, despite th e changes, support for Anzac Day as a day
of commemoration has built over time, and people’s understanding of the importance of
Waitangi Day has also increased. Nothing in this bill will change that.
Anzac Day will still be on 25 April. Dawn Serv ices will still be held. Large crowds
will still turn up to services and para des throughout the country. I will attend and
remember my father and grandfather, w ho fought in World War I and World War II.
Anzac Day will still be observed as a holiday on that day, regardless of which day of the
week it is, and people who work on that  day—and many do—will be paid time and a
half, and they will get a different day off,  with pay. Waitangi Day has a much more
recent history, but its significance as a day of celebration and commemoration on 6
February will also remain the same in the same way Anzac Day will.
But to take the National Party’s argument to its logical extension, nobody in this
country should be able to work on Anzac Da y or Waitangi Day, because those days are
just too sacred. But during this  debate I have not heard one  word of concern from the
National Party for the thousands of work ers who have to work on Anzac Day and
Waitangi Day.
There has been not one word of recogniti on that many workers do not get a holiday
at all and that for them Anzac Day and Waitangi Day are already on different days—not
one word from the National Party. There has been not one word of ownership of the
petty and distrustful extens ion of employer power that the National Government
introduced in 2010, where employers can tr ansfer Anzac Day and Waitangi Day to a
different day without the c onsent of workers—not one wo rd of concern from the
National Party about this. Instead, there has been a whole lot of sanctimonious concern
that somehow having a holiday, having these days Mondayised 1 year in 7—2 days out
of every 7 years—is going to undermine the sanctity, the sacredness, of Anzac Day. The
National Government brought in legislation in 2010 that a llows employers to decide
when Anzac Day falls or Waitangi Day falls and allows employers to decide when
workers get the days off. Anzac Day for th em can be any day other than 25 April.
Waitangi Day for them can be any day other than 6 February.
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9463
So, let us face it, for thousands of worker s in New Zealand there is no Anzac Day or
Waitangi Day. It is meaningless, and for th is Government to argue that this bill
undermines those holidays is, quite frankly—a word that I am not allowed to use. The
National Government has done away with Anzac Day and Waitangi Day for them, and
now it has been crying croc odile tears. Simon O’Connor was the best—10 minutes of
reading from the diary of a World War I sold ier. Unbelievable. Yet it was the National
Government’s legislation in 2010 that means that those 2 days just do not exist for many
workers. They work on the days and they ge t other days off that the employer decides
on. Anzac Day and Waitangi Day can be any days that the employer has decided on.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: It’s worse if they’re an independent contractor.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes, of course—there are some people who get no holidays,
like independent contractors, and that is another story.
Then we have had all the arguments ar ound cost. David Bennett made a bit of a
feeble attempt at it. I cannot accept that New Zealand is in such a bad state, that our
businesses are so, so hard up that this will send businesses broke, as the Government
has claimed, even to the extent of using it s dodgy figures. It is far more honest to just
accept and own up to the fact th at it does not want worker s to have more holidays.
Employer organisations like the Employers and Manufacturers Association were very
honest with us. When we as ked the association whether it had ever supported more
holidays, it at least owned up in the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee and
said no, it has never supported 4 weeks, ne ver supported extra holidays—just like the
National Government.
Then, as support has gathered for this bill, John Key has tr ied to do this “What, me
worry?” routine—“The world’ s not going to end.” I thin k the Government is now
embarrassed that it opposed this bill. It knows that it is on the wrong side of public
opinion. It knows it cannot justify its opposition, because it has already changed the law
to undermine the special natu re of Waitangi Day and Anz ac Day. I believe that the
Government knows in its heart of  hearts that this bill is the right thing to do. It is a
sensible bill. Kiwis know this is a fair deal. This is a great day for Kiwi workers. This is
a great day for Dr David Clark. It is wonde rful to see a Labour bill that will advance
things for New Zealand workers in this Hous e again. In 2014 there will be a lot more
when we are the Government.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Mike Sabin. Tēnā koe.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Thank you. Kia ora. I appreciate the
greeting. Can I firstly take an opportunity just to acknowledge David Clark, the member
introducing this bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day)
Amendment Bill, and—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The reverend doctor.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: That is the one. As I now understa nd, I can always rely on the Hon
Trevor Mallard to correct me if I go astra y—very helpful, very helpful. I do appreciate
having a wing man with such integrity. Can I acknowledge Grant Robertson also, as the
original author of this bill, and the Tran sport and Industrial Relations Committee. I am
now a member of that select committee, but I was not involved in th is process. It is
worthy of acknowledging the fact that when any member sees legislation pass through
this House, there has been a lot of hard work undertaken in that.
However, as members will be aware, the National Party will not be supporting this
bill. For me it comes down to quite a fine balance. First and foremost for me, as a
former naval officer and servicema n, the recognition of Anzac Day—the full
recognition of Anzac Day—is not something th at requires Mondayisation. Let us make
it very clear that Anzac Day needs no form of recognition other than the fact that it is
9464 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
Anzac Day, a time at which this nation gathers together to remember the sacrifices and
the lives that were lost in 1915 in Gallipoli, and all the other conflicts in which New
Zealand servicemen have upheld the honour of  this country and democracy. That is
something that I do not believe needs a public holiday in order to be recognised.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: It already is a public holiday.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, it certainly does not need  Mondayisation. I will come to that
member’s points in due course.
For me, the special significance of that day runs  the risk of being lost in the idea of a
public holiday—a 3-day weekend being the reason for celebration. And as we say
goodbye to the last of those most senior ve terans, it falls upon th e next generation and
their children to pick up that baton and carry it as we remember those who survived
those wars and have passed on. For me, that is something that ce rtainly does not need
the recognition of a bill such as this, which, really, in its title underpins, I think, exactly
what it is about: the Holidays (Full R ecognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day)
Amendment Bill. It somehow suggests that th ere is not adequate recognition of those
days, and that by making it a long weeke nd we will somehow more fully recognise
them. I believe that that is unnecessary.
As to the question of Waitangi Day, as a me mber of Parliament for Northland, again,
it is a very, very special and significant day for the nation. It is a day that has seen some
controversy. I remember as a policeman one or two battles of  the bridge, as we used to
call them up there, but I have to say that on the last Waitangi Day, this year in 2013,
there was definitely a change of mood at th at place where the Trea ty was signed. None
the less, it is a very, very significant day to this nation. It signifies the modern New
Zealand that we know now. It  was a starting point for th at. And as a member of
Parliament for that area, it is very important  for me that that day is recognised for what
it actually is.
Some have referred to it as New Zealand Day. In fact, members of the Labour Party
in years gone by have done that. I want to read just a couple of quotes from Hansard
that reflect the sentiment of the Labour Party of old. It may have some views as to what
today’s Labour Party is about. I will leave that for the punters out there to speculate on.
Former Minister of M āori Affairs Matiu Rata said: “Like Anzac Day, New Zealand
Day is not to be Mondayised. It is the si gnificance of the occasion that is important
rather than the fact that it is to be a paid  public holiday. It shoul d not be regarded as
merely an extra paid holiday.” That is one of them.
We heard the member Darien Fenton, w ho spent most of her 10-minute speech
talking about workers, holidays, and so on  and so forth, and although everyone will
accept that an honest, hard day’s work deserv es recognition in terms of a break, again I
come back to my original point about what  these days are actua lly about, what they
mean in the hearts and minds of New Zeala nders, versus becoming some default setting
as another holiday, another long weekend.
It goes on, because former Minister of Inte rnal Affairs Mr May, also of the Labour
Party, said: “The Government believes the Mondayising of New Zealand Day … would
detract from the importance and significance of the event it commemorates.” Former
MP Paraone Rēweti said that the committee considered that it was justified—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Who?

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Do you want me to write that down for you, Mr Mallard?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I will send it over in a note for you.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Where does he come from?

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am sure you know. You must be a great author of the Labour Party
history, I am sure. That member certainly carved his name well into it.
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9465

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I think he was here.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Yeah, well, that is good. Then th e member should know, so there is
no need to ask me. I am sure he can make a mental note for himself. Mr Rēweti said that
the committee considered that it was justified in declaring that Waitangi Day should not
be Mondayised, because the Labour Party had gone to the electors in 1972 on the policy
that Waitangi Day would not be Mondayised. If the member Trevor Mallard was here,
he probably remembers a lot of those speeches. He probably remembers what the old
Labour Party, the working Labour Party of old, was all about.
But I come to my point, which the member Darien Fenton has raised, and it is about
the consistent attack, as she puts it, by th e New Zealand National Party on the workers.
That is ironic given that the member w ho introduced this bill , David Clark, also
introduced the Minimum Wage Amendment B ill, which sought to raise the minimum
wage to $15 an hour. If we could just legislate the minimu m wage without any
consequence to the employer, who ultimately has to find the means to employ that
person, then why stop at $15? Why not c huck $25, $50, or maybe $100 an hour? That
member David Clark considers himself to be the best spokesman on economics in 50
years, and yet he has been a member who has single-handedly introduced two members’
bills to this House, both of which have a significant fiscal consequence to the employer.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: No, they don’t.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: They do. Of course they do.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: No, they don’t.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, I am not going to listen to the union strongman over there
bellowing his comments from across the floor , because at the end of the day—and that
member would have to recognise this—at so me point, employers need to find money to
pay their employees. To do that they have to be actually making a profit, and there is a
very fine line there. So the member who has introduced this bill, the so-called economic
spokesperson, will actually be hurting small and medium sized businesses. That is what
that is about.
Can I just close by saying that I acknowle dge the work that David Clark has done. I
respect the parliamentary process that has b een followed here, and for me this has been
about a fine balance. It has been a very fine balance.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: You know you want to vote for it. Come on, Mike.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: No, I certainly will not be. I certainly will not be. It has been a fine
balance, and for me it falls on the side of thos e servicemen in particular. As we
approach Anzac Day can I just acknowledge those fallen soldiers and servicemen from
across New Zealand who have served this c ountry so well in upholding our place in the
world and doing our bit and far more, those veterans who have survived those wars, and
the existing servicemen who are out there serving our country today.
On Anzac Day I will proudly be standing there to commemorate and to acknowledge
those people. I wonder whether Mr Clark will be confronted with a little bit of flack as a
result of this bill. Can I close by saying th at Anzac Day is a very important day to all
New Zealanders, and I look forward to this  Anzac Day to celebrate, commemorate, and
remember those who have fallen. Lest we forget.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: T ēnā koe. I am pleased to ta ke a short call on this
Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Da y and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill to
affirm the Green Party’s support for this very good bill. Our compliments to whatever
combination of Labour hearts and minds brought it into being. It is a very well-thought-
out and quite simple piece of legislation. It simply affirms that every year New
Zealanders will enjoy 11 public  holidays rather than having them in only 5 years out of
7 years, and missing out in those other 2 years.
9466 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
I am genuinely surprised that Govern ment members have not come round to
supporting this legislation. I have listened re asonably carefully to their speeches in
various readings, and that is not always an enjoyable experience, listening to speeches
from that side of the House, but it has been interesting to just try to unpick what their
objections are.
My fellow Northlander Mike Sabin, who just  resumed his seat, gave a very sincere
speech reflecting on his commitment to Anzac Day. I would have to say that if I
thought, or if any of my Green colleagues th ought, that the passing of this legislation
would in any way diminish or degrade th e importance or the integrity of that
celebration, we would probabl y not—well, in fact, I can say certainly I would not
support it, and I suspect neither would my colleagues.
Anzac Day is critically important. I confe ss in my former life I was more or less
committed to attending services on any given Anzac Day. As an MP I have also seen it
as an absolute duty to turn up at local celebrations, and also a pleasure. It is an
important day in our history and one we should continue to acknowledge.
The proposition that somehow Mondayising Anzac Day will lead to less commitment
to it and a smaller turnout to honour that day is at odds with the evidence from Australia
where Mondayisation has been in place for some time, and the numbers, if anything, are
increasing for attendances at Anzac Day celebrations, as indeed they are here in New
Zealand as younger people realise this is not ab out the glorification of war. It is about
acknowledging sacrifice and also a commitme nt to doing everything we can to avoid
wars in the future.
Some of the objection to this bill has been around the ec onomic effect—the effect on
business. Again I simply do not see that as being valid. We heard some extraordinary
numbers in the first reading, about the tens of millions of dollars  it would cost the
country every year to have two more days off, 2 years out of 7 years. Those numbers
simply do not add up. Some businesses will close, obviously, on days that otherwise
they would not, but that is more than comp ensated for in the scheme of things around
the larger economic picture by the fact th at the Mondayisation will enable people to
have extra time off. Long weekends will become feasible. There will be a knock-on
effect in tourism and elsewhere. So we  do not accept that there is any economic
difficulty or issue involved in that.
It contributes to our work-life balance. New Zealanders actually work some of the
longest hours of any developed country in th e world. Unfortunately that does not flow
through to productivity, which I will say a little more about in a moment, but we are just
making sure that we do maximise the work- life balance opportunities for people in the
workplace, and this bill does make a small but useful contribution towards that.
Mr Bennett seemed concerned that the bi ll did not go far enough, that somehow its
effect was so little as to not warrant his s upport. I am somewhat tempted to dust off the
Green Party’s April Fool’s Day spoof that suggested another eight holidays per year.
We might find support for that from the MP from Hamilton. But it does seem an
extraordinary proposition that because this is a relatively minor matter, albeit a positive
matter, it cannot be supported for that reason.
I have mentioned Anzac Day, and Waitangi Da y too is an important observation in
our history. It is very important  to us collectively, and person ally it is an important day.
I have both M āori and P ākehā tupuna who put their names to that document, put their
signatures on it, so it has always been ve ry much a part of my personal DNA. While
living in the north—well, even before liv ing in the north—I have been a regular
attendee at Waitangi Day celebrations in Waita ngi. It is noticeable that where Waitangi
Day falls on a weekend you te nd to find a different atte ndance than through the normal
course of events. The day of the week on wh ich it falls does affect the attendance at
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9467
Waitangi, people’s travel arrangements, and so on. The situation where it falls on a
Saturday or Sunday and people know that th e Monday is also a holiday will, I think,
enable more people to come to Waitangi and enjoy the celebration at that very key site.
It will do no harm for Northland tourism. As we know, Northland is one of the still
relatively undiscovered gems in the tourism crown of New Zealand. There is a great
deal to enjoy there. There is an incr easing supply of tour ism attractions and
accommodation, and I would encourage people who are heading north to hang around a
while and see just what a great deal there is to offer in the north.
I mentioned the issue of holidays—the fact th at people seem to think that if we have
one more holiday in each of those 2 years that somehow there will be an economic cost
to that. As to the number of holidays New Z ealanders have, be they large or small—you
can argue about whether 11 is  a lot or a few—our key eco nomic issue around that is
actually productivity. We do not have a producti ve economy. The reason for that is that
the one significant, and proba bly the single most important, contributor to that low
productivity is poor labour produc tivity. I believe firmly that the reason for that is that
we have a very poor management culture in  New Zealand. We have too many people in
management positions who are actually not good at that task. We have this unfortunate
habit of promoting people who might be good at  a particular activity to a management
role. This has been acknowledged by empl oyer groups, by employee groups, by the
finance sector, by bankers, and by a whole array of different sectors and different
interests in the economy.
The issues are not about whether we have 11  days off a year, or only 9, or 10. The
issue is that we do not invest enough in management and upskilling our managers in
New Zealand. If we invest a little bit there we  will get a great deal more productivity in
our economy. People perhaps could stop workin g such extraordinarily long hours, with
no economic cost, and in fact with significant economic benefit.
All in all, as I sai d, the Greens have been pleased to support this legislation from the
beginning. We will continue to offer that su pport, and we look forward to in future
years enjoying with the rest of New Zealand the time that it will allow for people to
maintain work-life balance, to spend time with their families, and to enjoy this beautiful
country of ours. We commend this bill to the House. Kia ora.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a great pleasure to  take a call on the Holidays
(Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. This is a very
important bill.
I want to acknowledge the work of Dr David Clark, my colleague, who picked up
this bill from Grant Robertson and also fr om Darien Fenton. I wanted to add that,
because, as we know, success has many fath ers and failure is an orphan. Although, of
course, when I say success has many fathers, I might say in light of the debate yet to
come that success has many parents, and for th ose who have just tuned in their radios
and their TVs, when I say success has many pa rents, I am talking in relation to the
Mondayisation bill. I am not pr omoting polygamy; I am just saying, as a saying, that
success has many parents and failure is  an orphan. My contribution to the
Mondayisation bill, which we are debati ng now, is that Grant Robertson had a
conversation with me as he was drafting it, so I feel that even my paw prints sit over this
very important piece of legislation.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I’m sure all of us talked to him while he was drafting it. Was
it about this?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Well, I am not saying he talked to me exclusively about it, but
I feel as if—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: But did he discuss the bill with you?

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: He discussed the bill with me even before I arrived here.
9468 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
I do not want to get into conspiracy theo ries about the old Labour Party and being
driven by the unions, because that certainly was not the ca se. But, in response to my
colleague Mike Sabin’s arguments about the ol d Labour Party versus the new, I want to
say about the old National Party that when it comes to labour rights, it was the old
National Party that actually introduced the first personal grievance law in this House, in
1970. That was a National Party that respec ted workers and workers’ organisations.
That was a National Party that actually wanted workers to have a good relationship with
their employer, to be respected, and to have fair processes. What a sea change we have
in the National Party of today, and perhaps I will come back to that when I have a
moment.
What I also want to say to Mike Sabin is that this bill is not about not observing
Anzac Day and Waitangi Day on the days they fall. Of course we will continue to do
that. These are important days . These are the days, and, i ndeed, the events that sit
behind them, that define us as a nation. We will always observe them, and we will
observe them with great emotion, great co nsideration, and great compassion towards
those who have gone before us for the contri bution they have made in the case of each
of them. But what this does do, at least in rela tion to those years in which the days fall
on a weekend day—actually observing the following Monday as a holiday enhances our
observation of them, and the commemoration or the celebration of those particular days.
This bill fulfils the promise of the Holiday s Act, which is to grant 11 days’ public
holiday to every worker, every year. That is an important thing and an important
achievement. It fulfils the promise of a m odern and civilised society and an economy
that not only recognises the contribution of  working people but recognises important
events in our history and allows us, as  a community, to commemorate them and
celebrate them as appropriate.
Let us not forget that in around about the last 15 years,  there has been a 25 percent
increase in productivity and value in this country, wherea s real wages have increased
barely 10 percent over the same period of time . There is no loss to business, not in any
aggregate sense at least, anyway. There is no loss to business in the 2 years out of 7
years that this bill will allow extra days to be granted to work ers in observation and
commemoration of these very important days. As David Clendon said in his
contribution, we are a nation that over the la st 20 years has shown that we are working
longer hours, on average, and we are not being paid commensurately for those
additional hours. We are not getting the rewa rd. This might be seen, for those who see
some economic difficulty in it, to provide just some little extra reward for those extra
hours worked and the extra productivity produced in our economy as a whole.
The truth is that this bill has widesp read support across New Zealand, not only
amongst working people but across many busin esses, not the least of which is the
Tourism Industry Association, which represen ts literally hundreds of businesses, big
and small, in this economy. It  has a very important role to  play. In fact, the tourism
industry is so important that this Govern ment is about to grant an additional $158
million over 4 years to it. That is how mu ch importance this Government sees the
tourism industry having. Quite why it does not  listen to it on issues like this, I do not
understand, although I can explain it when I go back to the issues about the modern
National Party and its attitude to workers and workers’ rights.
Responsible regulation in the labour market simply means ensuring fairness. This bill
is an example of responsible regulation, and it is a bill that will ensure greater fairness
for working people. This bill adds that. This bill—what it does; all it does—adds a
maximum of 2 days’ leave in 2 years out of every 7 years—2 years out of every 7 years.
This is not going to break the bank of Ne w Zealand productivity, or the bank of New
Zealand business. It is a fair recognition of something that, actually, our Holidays Act
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9469
already promises but does not, so far, deliver.  This will continue genuine observance of
these important commemorative days when they would otherwise fall on a weekend.
Let us talk about Anzac Day, because we are on the eve of Anzac Day week. When
we think about Anzac Day, we know that young New Zealanders, predominantly men—
in fact, it was all men—were conscripted into the army to  go and fight thousands of
miles away. That is important to us, because  actually one of the driving forces for the
founding of the Labour Party was an oppos ition to conscription. Young men were
conscripted to fight in a war many thousands of miles away. They accepted the
argument that this was for Queen and count ry, it was for a lifesty le, and it was for a
sense of freedom. It was not to work longer hours. It was not to lift their productivity by
25 percent and get nothing for it. That is not what young soldiers fought for in World
War I. They fought for a set of values and for greater freedom, and this bill properly and
truly recognises the sacrifice that was made , because it represents greater freedom—the
freedom to spend time with one’s family a nd the freedom to express oneself how one
wishes in one’s own time.
That is what this bill does, and we should respect it and support it  for that reason. It
is about putting work in balance with the rest of one’s life. That is the challenge of life
in the modern world, and this bill will help us  to achieve that. It is about good rights at
work.
When we think about Waitangi Day, and we th ink about the historical origins of that
day and about rights to citizen ship, this bill is about conf erring not only citizenship but
“humanship”, if you like. It is about the human ity of each of us—the right to have time
off to mark important historical events, to  commemorate them within our communities,
and to celebrate them where that is required. When we think about k āwanatanga and
tino rangatiratanga, working longer hours and being deprived of the right to observe
those important days is not what the Treaty of  Waitangi stands for. It stands for people
being people, and that, if anything, is what the Treaty of Waitangi is about—people.
So this bill is very important. This bill is very important, because it is a chance for us
to express our nationhood and those 2 importa nt days on a real day by having the world
of commerce stop for a moment and take a step back in years in which it would
otherwise not do so on these 2 important days, so that we can all observe them.
I started this contribution by talking about the new National Party. Look at
everything it has done when it comes to work rights. Every time this Government comes
to turn its attention to work rights, it is about taking away. It is a bout detracting from
workers and their rights, whether it is the 90- day trial period, whether it is changing the
test on personal grievances—a piece of law that actually or iginated from a progressive,
liberal National Party, which we do not have today and we do not have any more. When
we think about access rights at work, when we think about the rights of workers to have
a say over when they take their holidays, ev ery time this Government turns its attention
to work rights, it takes something away from workers.
Well, thank goodness for the Labour Party. Thank goodness for the Labour Party,
and at least in Oppos ition, with good members like Gr ant Robertson, Dr David Clark,
and Darien Fenton, we have the ability to in troduce laws like this and get them passed
for the good of all New Zealand. That is why we are supporting this bill.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Ng ā
mihi nui ki a koe i t ēnei ahiahi. I te w ā tuatahi i t ū au m ō tēnei o ng ā pire i te tau kua
hipa ake, anei taku kōrero: “I a tātau e kōrero nei mō tēnei o ngā pire, e rua ngā take nui
whakaharahara, e pīrangitia nei e au, m ātau o te Pāti Māori hei whakatakoto ki mua i te
aroaro o te Whare P āremata. Tuatahi ko t ērā o ng ā waiata, ng ā karanga nei me k ī,
‘honour the Treaty’, t ērā kōrero. Ka rua, ko te āhuatanga o te waihotanga mai o T ā
Apirana Ngata i te wā i a ia. Arā, ko tana kōrero, ko “the price of citizenship”. Ēnei take
9470 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
katoa, ‘honour the Treaty’, ‘the pr ice of citizenship’, kei reira tonu t ētahi hononga ki
waenganui i ngā kaupapa e rua i roto i tēnei pire.” Koinā taku kōrero i te wā i tū ake au i
te pānuitanga tuatahi o tēnei o ngā pire.
Ko tā mātau aronga nui mō tēnei o ngā pire ko tērā e pā ana ki ngā kaupapa e rua nei,
ko Te Tiriti o Waitangi ka mutu, ko te r ā o T ūmatauenga, ar ā, e k ī ana te k ōrero ko
Anzac; kaua ko te aronga ki te moni ka kore e kitea e te p ūkoro o ng ā kaituku mahi;
kaua ko te haerenga ki tātahi ki reira ruku kina ai, pāinaina rānei i te rā ēngari, ko te tino
pūtake o tēnei o ngā whenua i ahu mai ai i roto i te āhuatanga o Te Tiriti o Waitangi, ka
tahi, nā wai, n ā wai ko te r ā o Anzac, ar ā, te rā o T ūmatauenga e iri nei i te pakitara ā-
whare i tēnei wā.
Kei reira tonu kei te W āhanga 4 o t ēnei pire te p ūtake o tēnei pire. Kia huri ki te reo
Pākehā mō te wā poto. In clause 4 of this bill, the aim is “to amend the … [Holidays Act
2003] to provide for the transfer of the public holidays for Waitangi Day and ANZAC
Day if they fall on a weekend.” Ko te tino p ūtake o t ēnei pire, me k ī, te tikanga ia e
hāngai tonu ana ki t ēnei mea te kotahitanga o Aotearoa. E k ī ana ētahi, he iwi kotahi
tātau, e k ī ana ētahi, ko te whakakotahitanga o Aotearoa, P ākehā mai, M āori mai. Ki a
mātau, koinei kei te tino pūtake o tēnei pire.
Ka mutu t ērā pea, ka kitea mai ai ko te h ōhonutanga o t ēnei kaupapa, m ēnā i tiro, i
kite tātau i te Pouaka Whakaata Māori i te tau kua hipa, arā, i te wā i whakanuia ai ko te
rā o Anzac. I taua wā, i taua hōtaka, i kite mātau, tātau pea; ko Mātai Smith i te Kāreti o
Te Aute t ērā o ng ā kura rongonui o Te Ao M āori. I te w ā o nehe, ko Te Aute t ētahi o
ngā kura tino rongonui. An ā, ko ētahi o ng ā tama i haere ki t āwāhi, otirā, i eke atu ki
roto i te 28, arā, ko te 28th Māori Battalion. E ai ki tāku e mōhio nei, 250 ngā tama o tērā
kura i haere i raro i te parirau o te 28  ki te Pakanga Tuarua o te Ao. Ko t ētahi o rātau ko
Te Moananui-a-Kiwa Ngārimu. Ko ia tērā i whiwhi nei i te R īpeka o Wikitōria mō tōna
māia i te mura o te ahi.
Nā, i a au otir ā, i a t ātau pea e m ātakitaki ana i t ērā; ka rongo koe i te ng ākaunui o
ngā tama Māori ki ngā āhuatanga o te hunga i tae atu ki tērā kura, o te hunga i haere anō
hoki ki t āwāhi ki te mura o te ahi. I whakanuia ko te 28. Ki taku m ōhio, koinei te
āhuatanga o Te Ao M āori, ahakoa p ēhea te āhuatanga o t ēnei mea o te pakanga: ko te
ngākau o Te Ao M āori tino kaha whai nei, whakanui nei i te 28. N ā runga i te aha? N ā
runga i ngā kōrero i puta mai i te wā i a rātau e haere ana ki tāwāhi.
He pērā anō hoki ki Te Tai Tokerau, arā, ki Whangarei, ki tētahi kaupapa hōu nei kua
tipu ake i ngā tau kua hipa, ko te Leadership Academy o Kamupene A; tētahi wāhanga o
te 28. Ki taku m ōhio, 18 ng ā tama o roto o Whangarei e whai nei i ng ā tapuwae o te
28—he tamariki, he āhua tamariki nei. Ko te tikanga o te haere ki t ēnei kaupapa, t ēnei
akoranga, tēnei academy, ko te tika o te t ū, ko te aronganui ki te tangata, ko te m āia, ko
te angitu ki te whai kaupapa ki tōna mutunga.
Ko ētahi o ng ā tama i roto i t ēnei kaupapa, ar ā, te leadership academy, ko r ātau ngā
uri o te hunga i haere ki tāwāhi. He māia te tū, āhua rite, me kī, ki a Tūmatauenga i tōna
pūtake kia tika te kākahu, ka tirohia te āhuatanga o ngā moenga ka mutu, ko te pakari ā-
tinana ēnei āhuatanga katoa. Koinei ng ā kaupapa ka whaiwhai haeretia e t ēnei hunga.
Ko te aronganui kia t ū Māori tonu ēnei tama, kia m ōhio mai ai ko wai r ātau, kia mōhio
mai ai ko te waihotanga mai o te hunga kua ngaro i te tirohanga kanohi, kia mōhio rātau
he uri nō tērā hunga, he uri n ō ngā rangatira i haere ki tua o te pae ēngari, ko te hunga i
haere ki te pakanga. N ā, mā ēnei akoranga ka mōhio mai ai he r ā nui, whakaharahara te
rā o Anzac. Ka mutu, ko ēnei uri e whai nei i t ērā kaupapa i t ēnei rā tonu nei, ahakoa,
arā, kei te whakanui tātau i te hunga kua ngaro.
Kia hoki mai au ki Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Ki taku m ōhio, ka whakaiti t ātau i te tino
pūtake o tēnei pire mēnā ko t ā tātau ko te nui o te utu ki runga i ng ā tāngata tuku mahi
ki tēnā, ki t ēnā. Ka aroha hoki i te mea, kei te whakanui t ātau i te hunga i mate m ō te
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9471
painga o Aotearoa. Kei reira te tino kaupapa nui. Kaua ko te pūtea i tōna kotahi, kaua ko
te whakat ā i t ōna kotahi ēngari me hoki mai t ātau ki te kotahitanga o t ēnei whenua o
Aotearoa. Ka p ūtake mai t ō tātau h ītori i te āhuatanga o te nohotahi o t ātau o Te Ao
Pākehā me t ātau o Te Ao M āori i raro i Te Tiriti o Waitangi. N ō reira, he kaupapa nui
tēnei.
Me kī, 5 tau kua hipa ka puta te k ōrero i a Carol Archie, he kaituhi t ēnei wahine i
Waitangi ia, ka mutu, i puta t ētahi k ōrero i a ia m ō te āhuatanga o te kaupapa nei o
Waitangi. Anei tana kōrero, ka huri ki te reo P ākehā. Carol Archie, about 5 years ago at
Waitangi, said these words: “People in Māori/ Pākehā families say it’s not easy to either
marry someone from another culture or to be the children of such a union. But most
enjoy being able to walk between cultures with comfort and the chance to understand
life from different perspectives. I feel ex cited about it because they’re doing the
groundwork to help us unde rstand who we’re becomi ng as a nation.” Taku m ōhio me
pērā wā tātau whakaaro m ō te āhuatanga o t ā tātau noho. Ar ā anō ngā Minita M āori e
kōrerohia ake nei i p ūtake mai ai i Ingarangi, ar ā, ko Dover Samuels t ērā nō roto
Ingarangi. Ko Sharples, n ō te clan o Bolton i Ingarangi. Ko w ā tātau mokopuna he
kahurangi ngā karu. Ka moe te P ākehā i te M āori, te M āori i te P ākehā, kei reira tonu
wā tātau whakapapa e whakakotahi nei i raro i te āhuatanga o te aroha o tētahi ki tētahi.
Ka mutu, kai hea ēnei kōrero e haere ana? Ko t āku, ko te tino painga o t ēnei momo
pire mō te kaupapa o Dr David Clark, ko t ēnei private member’s bill kua whakatuwhera
nei i te āhuatanga o te k ōrero o te kotahitanga o Aotearoa. Koin ā tētahi o ng ā tino
painga. M ā reira kua m ōhio t ātau ki ō tātau h ītori, ka mutu, kei te tino ngako o t ēnei
pire, ko wā tātau nohotahitanga ka mutu, ko te kaupapa nui o Te Tiriti o Waitangi i roto
i wā tātau kōrero.
Ehara i te mea he nui ng ā kōrero i tua atu o t ērā. N ā mātau te k ōrero ki te David
Clark nei, te mema nei āe, ka tuku te P āti Māori i ōna pōti e toru. Āhua uaua i ētahi wā
nā te mea, kua puta ētahi o ng ā Minita, kua hoki mai ētahi Minita ēngari, ko t āku ki te
mema, ki a Mr Grant Robertson, i t ēnei wā koirā te waha kōrero, te tangata i w āwāhi i
ngā kōrero, kei te whakaae atu te P āti Māori ki te tuku i te p ōti tautoko i t ēnei pire, me
te mihi ki te mema n āna an ō tēnei kaupapa i k ōkiri ki mua i te aroaro o te Whare
Pāremata. He mea pai t ēnei. Ko tā te Pāti Māori he tautoko, he tautoko, he tautoko. Kia
ora tātau.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Huge salutations to you. When I rose for the first time to
speak at the first reading of this bill last year, this is what I said: “As we debate this bill
there are two concepts that we, the M āori Party, wish to present before Parliament.
Firstly, there is the activist chant ‘honour the Treaty’, and, secondly, there is the legacy
of Sir Apirana Ngata’s phrase ‘the price of citizenship’. Both are connected intimately
in this bill.” That was in my address at the first reading of this bill.
Our main focus as far as this bill is concerned is on these two matters, the Treaty of
Waitangi and the God of War da y, otherwise referred to as Anzac Day. It is not about
employers being out of pocket, going to the beach to dive for sea urchins, or basking in
the sun, but rather because this country was founded on the principles of the Treaty of
Waitangi—that is one—and eventually, over time, Anzac Day, God of War day, which
adorn the walls of this chamber currently.
The essence of this bill is very much there in Part 4 of this bill. Let me turn to
English for a short moment. In clause 4 of  this bill, the aim is “to amend the …
[Holidays Act 2003] to provide for the trans fer of the public holidays for Waitangi Day
and ANZAC Day if they fall on a weekend.” The real essence or meaning of this bill,
shall we say, relates directly to the unity  of New Zealand. According to some, we are
one people; others say it is the oneness of New Zealand, P ākehā and Māori. To us, this
is the real crux of this bill.
9472 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
Furthermore, the depth of th is matter would have been no ted if we looked at and
watched Māori Television last year when Anzac Day was being celebrated. At that time
on that programme we—all of us, perhaps—saw that M ātai Smith was attending that
famous school of Māoridom Te Aute College. Te Aute was one of the greatest schools in
the past. Some of the boys went  overseas, enli sted in the 28 th Māori Battalion. My
understanding was that 250 students of that school served under the wing of the 28 th
Battalion in the Second World War. One of them was Te Moananui-a-Kiwa Ng ārimu.
He was the one awarded the Victoria Cross for his valour at the battle-front.
When I was—indeed, all of us, perhaps , were—watching that programme, you
experienced the commitment of those M āori boys who attended that school and the
commitment of those as well who went ove rseas to the battle-front. It was the 28 th
Battalion that was honoured. My understanding is that this is the situation in Māoridom
regardless of the nature of this th ing about warfare: feelings among M āoridom for the
28th Battalion are very, very strong. The battalion is celebrated greatly as well. On what
grounds? Because of the accounts that emerged at the time they were heading overseas.
It is like that as well up north in Whangarei in regards to one of these new initiatives,
the Leadership Academy of A Company, a division of the 28 th Battalion that has
developed over the past years. I understand there are 18 boys from within Whangarei
following in the footsteps of the 28th Battalion—mere children, youngish. The motive for
going to this scheme, training, academy is to become disciplined, focused on people,
bold, and successful in pursuing something to its conclusion.
Some of the lads in this leadership acade my are descendants of those who served
overseas. They stand with bearing just like one in the army, correctly dressed and
where beds are inspected. Furthermore, ther e is physical training and all these sorts of
things. These are matters that these young one s will address. The fo cus is that these
sons be M āori in every way, know who they are, know the legacy left by those who are
no longer alive, and know they are relatives  of theirs and of the esteemed ones who
have passed over the divide and went to the wa r. It is through thes e teachings that they
will become aware of how important and extraordinary Anzac Day is. Furthermore,
these are the relatives  who continue to pursue that aspect today even though we are
celebrating those who have gone.
Let me come back to the Treaty of Waitangi. To me, we will denigrate the real
purpose of this bill if we focus on how much employers pay each worker. I empathise
because we are commemorating those who di ed for the good of New Zealand. And that
is where the real crux of the matter is. It  is not about the money or the holiday on its
own; we need to come back to the unity  of this country, Ne w Zealand. Our history
evolved from how we of P ākehādom and M āoridom lived under the auspices of the
Treaty of Waitangi. So this is an important matter.
Five years ago, shall we say, this woman Carol Archie, a writer, made a statement at
Waitangi about the situation there. Here is what she said. I will relate it in English.
Carol Archie, about 5 years ago at Waitangi , said these words: “People in M āori/
Pākehā families say it’s not easy to  either marry someone from another culture or to be
the children of such a union. But most enjo y being able to walk between cultures with
comfort and the chance to unde rstand life from different pe rspectives. I feel excited
about it because they’re doing the groundwor k to help us understand who we’re
becoming as a nation.” What I make of the si tuation is that our thinking about how we
live should be like that. There are other M āori Ministers referred to here, like Dover
Samuels, whose name originated from Engl and. The name Sharples is from the Bolton
clan in England. Our grandchildren have blue eyes. When a P ākehā marries a M āori,
and a Māori marries a P ākehā, our bloodlines are still th ere being combined under the
love of one for the other.
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9473
So where are these comments heading to? For me particularly, the real benefit of
this kind of bill bel onging to Dr David Clark, this priv ate member’s bill, is that it has
opened up discussions on the oneness of New Ze aland. That is one of its real benefits.
Through that we will understand our history, the gist of this bill, our living together as
one, and eventually the main theme of the Treaty of Waitangi in our comments.
There is not much more to add to the debat e. We assured this David Clark, this
member, that, yes, the M āori Party is going to cast its three votes. It is difficult
sometimes because Ministers come and go, but  I can assure the member Mr Grant
Robertson, who at this stage is pres iding over proceedings, that the M āori Party agrees
to cast its vote in favour of this bill and congratulates the member who brought this bill
before Parliament. This is  a wonderful outcome. The M āori Party supports, approves,
and endorses it. Congratulations to us collectively.]

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: On behalf of New Z ealand First I rise to
support the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment
Bill. New Zealand First is very pleased that this bill has now reached its final stages.
We would like to extend our congratulations  to Dr David Clark on having achieved a
real milestone with this bill. Very few Opposition MPs ever—ever—have one of their
bills pass into law from this side of the Hous e. It is a very rare event, so we are very
pleased. We are pleased, too, that there is wi despread support on this side of the House
for the whole bill, and we are very happy to share in Dr Clark’s success. We are sure
that there is some reluctant support across the other side of the House, as well, from the
National members, and I know their speeches have not had any really valid reasons as to
why this bill should not be supported.
Without a doubt, Dr Clark, or perhaps ev en Labour, will be on the minds of many
Kiwis up and down the country on 25 April 2015, th e very first year that is affected by
this legislation. Many will not remember or will  not even care, but they will be grateful
for the Mondayisation of Anzac Day. Like the majority of New Zealanders, New
Zealand First is really pleased to see this bill finally passing into law.
As it currently stands, we believe that Waitangi Day and Anzac Day have been given
second-class status among our  public holidays. It is si mply not good enough. We have
Mondayisation of Christmas Day and New Year ’s Day, and there have  been absolutely
no problems whatsoever, so there should be no problems forthcoming with the
Mondayisation of Anzac Day or Waitangi Da y. These 2 days stand out amongst our
annual holidays, in so far as they are app licable to all New Zealanders—each and every
one of us. Irrespective of background or cr eed, whether you grew here or flew here,
these are the 2 days that mark us all as New Zealanders. They are our 2 national days.
We have heard right throughout  the progression of this bi ll how much demand there
is for the full recognition of these days. Research shows that over 80 percent of New
Zealanders and the majority of businesses ha ve welcomed Dr Clark’s proposal in this
bill. It makes sense, it provides a consistency, it is a good deal for workers and for
businesses alike, and New Zealanders know this. The taxi driver who picked me up
from the airport this week said that he cannot  wait for this bill to pass into law. People
are talking about it. They value the role that holidays have. We know it is realistic to say
that New Zealanders do not work from 9 to 5 any more and this bill will help that work-
life balance.
Both Waitangi Day and Anzac Day will not have their symbolism eroded or their
special character taken away by these change s. On 6 February New Zealanders right
throughout the country will mark the date of  the signing of New Zealand’s founding
document. We will reflect on past inju stices. We will further reflect on the
reconciliation process and look at how we might best move forward as a united country
and a united people. Waitangi Day is something that sets New Zealand apart. It is a day
9474 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
of recognition of the past, of hope for the future, and of unity. The mere fact that
thousands of New Zealanders and expats in  London come together on Waitangi Day to
commemorate the occasion shows that even Kiwis overseas have got a really strong
affinity for this day. How could Mondayisation, having an extra day off if Waitangi Day
falls on the weekend, really pose a problem?
The other important day that is affected by this legislation is Anzac Day—another
one of our national days. It is a day on whic h we give thanks to those who paid the
ultimate price for protecting the liberties of New Zealanders and others. Next Thursday
we commemorate Anzac Day, and no doubt every single one of us in this House will
attend an Anzac Day service. The Anzac expe rience brought about a really strong bond
between New Zealand and Australia, recogni sing our common heritage, our geography,
and our way of life. An increasing number of people, and young people in particular, are
now attending Anzac Day dawn ceremonies. I know. I always attend my local Dawn
Service in my town. They are eager to learn about the history and the symbolism, and to
share in the sense of camaraderie on Anzac Day. Many of these young New Zealanders
proudly wear their great-grandfathers’ medals  on their chests, pinne d to their chests—
very proud.
It is very interesting to note that the same thing is happening in Australia. People
young and old are actively engaged in commem orating their heroes. All of this is
despite the fact that in Au stralia they have already M ondayised Anzac Day, with no
detrimental effect whatsoever. Kiwis up a nd down the country knew that they were
being robbed by a quirk of the system when they did not get their 11 days of public
holidays, and we always accepted it as a part of life. This bill is going to remedy this
anomaly and streamline how we treat public hol idays. On 2 days in  every 7 years there
will be the extra holiday.
The tourism industry supports this bill. They can see only positive outcomes from
this change, as people will travel to ot her centres around New Zealand that they
previously have not travelled to, or never had the time to actually travel to. This bill has
the support of workers, it has the support of businesses, it ha s the support of tourism,
and it definitely has the support of New Zealand First. Thank you.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak on the Holidays
(Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. I wish to
acknowledge the contribution of my collea gue Barbara Stewart, across the House—a
very eloquent presentation. However, it has not been enough to get me to change my
mind on this bill, despite the eloquence. I wi sh to acknowledge Grant Robertson and Dr
David Clark, because it is always a pleasure to  have a bill come before the House that
one has crafted, in Grant’s case—before he handed it on to Dr David Clark. I am hoping
to have my own bill come quite soon to this House, and I look forward to that. So I can
empathise with the work done by Dr David Clark.
Despite the eloquence of previous speakers, I have a visceral distaste for this bill, and
I was just searching back as to why this should be. I guess the reason comes from the
huge respect I have—and I am not suggesti ng other people in the House do not have
that—for members of our armed forces, men and women, who have served. Where does
this stem from? I spoke in the House some weeks ago on this very bill. My grandfather
served in the Boer War. So I grew up being aware of the sacrifices made by, actually,
thousands of New Zealanders very early in our history—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: The Boer war? Crikey.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: In the Boer War—in the Boer War.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Which side?

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: He was a member of the New Zealand Mounted Rifles. He had
to take his own horse, as I recall. He used to entertain me as a young lad with stories
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9475
upon his knee. As I was growing up—I lost my dad when I was 6—I was taught to
shoot, and I built a pram dinghy with my neighbour Ron Carr, now deceased, whom I
would like to pay tribute to in this House, who was a World War II veteran and who
also served in the Korean War. I remember playing in the back garden with a Japanese
jungle carbine that he had miraculously brought back from the campaign that he served
in. I learnt how to handle weapons with him,  going out shooting rabbits in the foothills
of Mount Egmont, as we used to call it th en, or Mount Taranaki. Both names pertained
at that stage. Look, this background is just trying to shape my distaste for this bill,
because I have always honoured this day. Anzac Day has stood alone—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: We all have.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: I know you are saying across the House that  it in no way
detracts—personally, I believe it was raised above other days of significance by the fact
that is was not always a holiday. I felt, and I have said it in this House before, that that
was a way we could give credit and acknowledge the sacrifice made by generations who
have gone before and who in many cases paid the ultimate price. Fo r us to give up a
holiday once in a blue moon is no sacrifice at all. So that is shaping my view.
