I also did a territorial officer selection board as a young lad and became a member of
“the blue berets”. As many of you know, “the blue berets” are the members of the Otago
University Medical Company who went off to  serve in Viet Nam. At the time when
they were called—two officers went every ye ar—I would have gone were it not for the
fact that, fortunately for the Viet Namese, the peace process intervened. For a young lad
from the Naki who was keen to go and serve in a medical corps, it was a huge
disappointment for me personally, but a grea t joy for everybody else  involved in that
horrible, ugly conflict. We were going to patch people up, not to lay waste to them.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: You’re not a very good shot.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: As has been pointed out by my colleague Todd McClay, with
one eye I probably wasn’t a very good shot, but  that was not what we were going there
for.
It is probably appropriate to mention th e extremely hard work done by one of the
legendary chairmen of select committees. I refer, of course, to David Bennett. David
Bennett is a legendary chairman of select committees and it was his Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee that saw the submissions and dealt with submissions.
Were there many? There were not many. In fact, only 32 submissions on this bill were
received: 18 submitters supported the bill and 12 submitters opposed the bill. The
chairman has actually pointed out that ther e were some good arguments for and against
this bill. There were arguments that came through in opposition to the bill. So what
were some of these key themes?
Well, as we have heard, the bill would create additional costs. And what would some
of these costs be? The cost to the employe rs estimated by the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment is an estimated  impact of $220 million to $280 million.
That is not insignificant. The cost to the whole economy output estimated by the New
Zealand Institute of Economic Research is $134 million to $186 million. These are not
insignificant. So that was one of the thought s. Some of the submitters thought that it
might diminish the significance of Waitangi Day and Anzac Day. It could create further
unfairness, it could create further confusion—these were some of the comments made—
and it could encourage a change in shift and roster patterns. Those were themes coming
out in opposition to the bill.
One of the submitters in opposition was Business New Zealand. If I can be a little bit
more specific here, some of the points it made in its submissions are as follows. In its
opposition to change it said there was little ba sis for change. I have to accept that. I
9476 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
mean, this is a meaty, beefy, big and bouncy, co mpact, and perky little member’s bill. I
have already paid my respects to Grant Robertson, and to Dr David Clark as well.
Anzac Day and Waitangi Day are noted by the submitters, Business New Zealand, as
being specific to New Zealand and as co mmemorative days. Business New Zealand
makes the point that “This is in contrast to Christmas Day and New Year’s Day which
are not”—and this is a surprising point, a nd it has a point here—“ days of significance
for every New Zealander.” It made that point in its submission.
Easter Monday is another example of another holiday contrasted with these days. In
this case, Easter Monday was created  to provide people with a holiday—[ Interruption]
Can we have a little bit of hush, please? It was created to provide people with a holiday
as it was previously uncommon to work on Easter Sunday. The submitter considers the
title of the bill to be “inapt”,  as the original purpose of both days was to recognise their
special nature. The submitter references the 1921 Anzac Day Amendment Bill and the
1960 Waitangi Day Act.
Business New Zealand did acknowledge, in its even-handed way, that the tourism
industry would benefit, but it noted that other businesses are concerned about the
potential costs, and we have  talked about how much th at would be. I notice that
Business New Zealand’s submission is suppor ted by the National Association of Retail
Grocers and Supermarkets of New Zealand. So there is a very strong submission, and
the overwhelming number of submissions were  actually against this. In contrast, the
tourism industry supports this bill, and it suggested that it may actually stimulate
domestic tourism, and would be affordable for business while increasing the importance
of Waitangi Day and Anzac Day.
One of the things that people have raised in the House, and in closing I would just
like to address this, is that  somehow it was thought that Ne w Zealand was out of step
with the rest of the world in the number of public holidays. Well, in fact, we are not.
The United States has 10, and no minimum annual paid leave. The United Kingdom has
eight. Australia has eight, and 20 days’ annua l paid leave—the same as New Zealand.
So there are arguments for and agin this bill, but I remain implacably opposed thereto.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: A split call. Five minutes, Carol Beaumont.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: It is a real pleasure  to rise and speak on a
positive and necessary bill that will pass here today. We have had far too many negative
bills in this House and we have had far too many pieces of legislation that are not, in
fact, necessary, but are really about dog whistle politics, like bashing beneficiaries. But,
anyway, I rise to speak on the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC
Day) Amendment Bill. I want to acknowledge , of course, Dr David Clark and Grant
Robertson, and also the Labour members of th e select committee, who worked hard on
this, as others have said—Darien Fenton, the senior member on the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee, and my colleague and friend here Andrew Little—all of
whom have contributed, I think, important points to this debate.
This bill came about as a re sult of a real problem. Someth ing in Parliament that we
are meant to be aware of is identifying th ings that need changing and addressing the
need for change. This was a real problem. Many people felt that in 2011 they had had
fewer holidays than they were entitled to, and, in fact, that was true. They had had 9
public holidays, rather than the 11 that they had expected.
The purpose of the bill is quite clear, and it is not all of the things that the National
MPs have been trying to say it is. They have been trying to run a line that somehow this
is going to undermine important days of na tional significance for us. I do not think they
have been successful, and I am sure that thos e listening to and watching the House have
not been convinced by their arguments, but I w ill come back to that. What this bill is
actually about is addressing an issue that ar ises only in those years when Waitangi Day
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9477
and Anzac Day fall on a weekend. It will amend the Holidays Act to provide for the
transfer of the public  holidays for Waitangi Day and Anzac Day if they fall on a
weekend.
The celebration of those very critically important days, which are fundamental to our
national identity, will still be, in the case of  Waitangi Day, 6 February and, in the case
of Anzac Day, 25 April, but there will also  be a public holiday on the Monday that
follows in those years when Waitangi Da y or Anzac Day fall on a weekend. That is
what it is really about. It is not about disrespecting those important days. Nobody here is
of that mind, and that is not what the bill doe s. It will ensure that certainly most New
Zealanders—full-time paid employees—will get 11 public ho lidays every year, rather
than in only 5 out of every 7 years.
This change, as others have said, is well supported. It is well supported by the public,
it is well supported by employ ees, and it is well supported by a number of employers—
particularly, as others have said, in the t ourism industry. But also one of the few pieces
of quantitative research done on this has shown that 87 percent of over 1,000 small and
medium enterprises that were surveyed act ually supported it or were neutral on the
question. So the argument that employers do not support this bill is nonsensical, and it
makes sense really, because thos e employers also have families  that they want to spend
time with.
Most New Zealanders, and, I would imagine, every member of this House, recognise
that holidays are important. Why are holidays important? We ll, let me spell it out.
Holidays are an opportunity for rest and r ecreation. Holidays help people balance paid
working time with time off to spend with family and friends. Let us recognise that in the
case of Anzac Day, those who fought for our country fought for our values, and that
includes the importance of family and mateshi p. We all know that those were critically
important to those Anzacs. So holidays are important, and they have become, arguably,
more important as paid work has become  more demanding for many. There are longer
hours, flexibility that makes it harder to balance work a nd life, and fewer people in
workplaces, which is intensifying work.
I want to acknowledge also, given that we are talking about paid work, the many,
many New Zealanders who are without paid work at the moment—who are
unemployed. I want to note again the Governme nt’s failure to focus on jobs, while it is
at the same time taking a puni tive approach to beneficiar ies. We have very high
unemployment—we have jobless growth at  the moment—but, on a rare occasion, we
are in this House celebrating something positive for those in paid employment, and I
commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: The Green Party is very pleased to support the Holidays (Full
Recognition of Waitangi Day and ANZAC Da y) Amendment Bill on its third reading
tonight, and we look forward to  it passing into law. We are supporting this bill for lots
of reasons, but primarily because we support a good work-life balance for New
Zealanders and we believe that the economy is a tool to serve our planet and our people,
and a good work-life balance is something that looks after us.
I would like to acknowledge Dr David Clark and Grant Robertson, my old boss, who
was never able to give me that Monday o ff. I know he would ha ve really loved to,
because his party has produced this wonderful  bill. The Greens would like to do a lot
more to support a balanced society—one where every New Zealander could have a
great life. Just imagine if we planned for our  economy to help us all have balanced and
fulfilling lives. Would that not be a beautiful thing?
This bill is actually  just a really tiny thing, a nd to be opposing it just seems
curmudgeonly to me, I have to say. We believe that this bi ll will enable workers and
their families to enjoy the full entitlement  of the Holidays Act—11 public holidays per
9478 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
year every year. Under the existing Holidays Act, in every 2 out of 7 years those 11
public holidays reduce to 9 days a year because Waitangi Day and Anzac Day are
celebrated on specific days.
We have other days on which the holidays happen on the same day every year, they
are marked, and people get a holiday on a di fferent day: Christmas Day, Boxing Day,
New Year’s Day, and the day after New Y ear’s Day. When those days fall on
weekends, the law allows for them to be transferred so that workers get the full
entitlement from those days. We recognise  the importance of doing that. The Greens
maintain that the difference in treatmen t between Waitangi Day and Anzac Day, and
Christmas Day, Boxing Day, New Year’s Day, and the days after those 2 days is an
anomaly.
We reject the notion put by some submitte rs and members across the House that it
will undermine either of those important days to have a holiday on a separate day. We
have not seen any evidence of this happeni ng with Christmas Day, and I do not think it
has any less meaning to us as a people because we have a holiday on another day.
Australia already transfers An zac Day to a Monday when it occurs on a weekend, and
the day’s commemorations are still held on 25 April. Even with Mondayisation, Anzac
Day events in Australia are really well atte nded, and I do not think that would change
here.
The majority of small businesses—I think all of us on this side of the House really
strongly support the interests of small busin esses—are supporting th is initiative. The
tourism industry, as has been noted, has said that it sees this as an opportunity to
increase domestic tourism and that the ec onomic benefits outweigh the costs to small
employers. That is, I think, a good thing. The co sts of this are not at all outrageous.
Employers already bear the costs of public holidays for their staff most years. Another 2
years is not going to break the bank.
I just want to talk a little bit about the f act that I think New Zealanders work really
hard—too hard, actually. I am not saying th is as a slacker. I am the product of a
Protestant work ethic and a workaholic fath er. I have never achie ved work-life balance
in my life without feeling I was letting myself or my employer down, to be honest, but I
recognise that to be disordered. I saw the really significant health costs on my father,
who needed to be resuscitated by my mother after he had a heart attack in his 40s, due
to not being able to achieve work-life bala nce, from being a workaholic. We have an
ever-increasing pressure on workers in this country, and they need to be looked after a
little better. This bill is a tiny step towards that.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I am very pleased to rise to speak on
the Holidays (Full Recognition of Waitangi  Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill.
The previous member, Jan Logie, was talkin g about small elements. I think what is
important is that she mentioned a few details  but, of course, missed the wider context.
People have been talking about  Australia and holidays, and so on. Well, in Australia,
just to look at a few facts, they have eight public holiday s a year and 20 days off by
right. In New Zealand, of course, we have 11  days off, not 8—we have 11. If this bill
passes through, we will move to 12 or 13 publ ic holidays along with 20 days off. The
US has only nine public holidays, and no mandated leave. Canada—just across the
border, of course, for those geographically  challenged—has nine  public holidays and
only 10 mandated days of leave.
So New Zealand already has 11. We have mo re public holidays th an all those other
countries. We have more public holiday s—a small detail for the Greens—than
Australia. If we pass this bill, then we m ove to have even more public holidays. That
can be right or wrong, but it is a context that does make New Zealand less competitive
in a global environment. It is really important that we provide the full context. So, to the
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9479
member who just resumed her seat, “curmudgeonly” can be an excellent word, I have to
say. Personally, I feel that the word “Monda yisation” is a crime against the English
language, and I feel terrible to even use it. But we need, obvious ly, to touch all the
details. It is very important.
I do not really want to get on to the economic front as we ll, because those who have
heard previous speeches of mine will know th ey have played more on the principle, but
the other side of it, too, is that there are al ways costs to decisions that are made. So we
have heard here in the House today, and it  was from Grant Robertson in his initial
speech, that—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: A brilliant speech!
SIMON O’CONNOR: Well, it was a speech, I will gi ve it that. He said we should
be giving and encouraging more holidays. We  hear also from Labour, the Greens, and
other parties that there is more we have to do, we have to pay people more money, and
there have to be more opportunities. Whether that is right or wr ong is one question, but
the other is always to admit there is a cost. Where there are more holidays, where there
is more pay, someone has to pay that price.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: And there are also benefits.
SIMON O’CONNOR : Kiwis have to pay that pr ice. Yes—I acknowledge the
interjection from Andrew Little—there are benefits, too. Bu t there are also costs, which
need to be acknowledged.
I do not support this bill. Th e reason remains very simple , as I said from my first
speech, and that is that Anzac Day and Waita ngi Day are not excuses for holidays. I
think it is important for ever yone to understand. It  has been iterated in the House a few
times that, of course, Anzac Day and Waitangi Day are holidays. It is not as if they are
not going to be or will be more so; they are holidays, be they on a Tuesday, a Thursday,
a Saturday, or a Sunday, and that remains. We will be able to attend our services, and so
on. But this has become a bill that wants to use those days of commemoration to be an
excuse for a day off. When we listen to  the Opposition, it does not take long at all
before tourism, barbeques, and other commercial enterprise usages kick up. I invited the
Opposition in my second reading speech—and this is an important point—to say to me:
“Look, we want to have a di scussion about more holidays. ” Then let us have that
discussion. Let us have that discussion. I said: “Let’s not use Anzac Day and Waitangi
Day as an excuse, but if we want to talk about more holidays, come and have a chat
with me.”

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: But they’re already holidays.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Here we are—and one of the Opposition members has yelled
out that they are already holiday s. Yes, that is right; they ar e already holidays. This bill
is saying that we should us e those existing holidays—t hose days of commemoration—
as an excuse for more holidays. I reject th at. I say: “Come up with better ideas.” They
should come up with better ideas. But to date not one person from the Opposition—not
one person from the Opposition—has come to talk about an opportunity to create new
holidays. No, they are more than happy to use these days of commemoration in this
way. And it will harm them. It does make changes to mindsets.
Principles are important. Consistency is important. That is lost on the Opposition
members, too, when they are saying that these are just the same—these days are just the
same as Christmas Day or Easter. They are not. They are not. Da ys like Christmas,
Easter, and so on are days of festivities. One needs just to look at the etymology of
where the words come from. They are days of celebration. But these days, Waitangi
Day and particularly Anzac Day, are days of commemoration. We have the ability
already in law, in stat ute, and by convention to undertake these days of
commemoration. This bill uses this as an ex cuse to create more. The Opposition yells
9480 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 17 Apr 2013
up and down that it might be only every so of ten, but that is not th e point. If you are a
person of principle, then you stick to principles and you stick to consistency. That is the
key operating here.
In a few days’ time, many of us right across the House will, of course, be
undertaking our Anzac Day obligations and duties with a heartfelt desire, and I am sure
that goes right across the House. I am very much looking forward to joining the people
of Tāmaki down in St Heliers Bay. We have a little war memorial there on the bay for a
young man. I think it is for Guyon Brookfield, who used to be a Scout troop leader, who
died in the First World War. A number of us right across T āmaki, from all the different
communities, will come together on the 25th to remember that day. I think it is important
to acknowledge that the day does remain a day of commemorati on. To be honest, I do
not expect any of those people in my electora te, standing there at the memorial, to say:
“Oh, Simon, you know, I wish we had an excuse for another day off.” It is not going to
happen.
We do not need this piece of legislation. What we need, as I have offered and
suggested before, is a free and frank conversatio n. If we want more holidays, then let us
have that discussion. Do not use Anzac Day. Do not use Waitangi Day. Just remember,
of course, what we began with. My colleague David Bennett, fine chairperson that he is,
has noted that New Zealand already has an incredibly good deal on holidays in
comparison with other countries  in the world. We are a great country. We already have
our systems well in place. I do not support the passage of this bill. I ask the members of
the Opposition to stand with a lot of Kiwis who have wri tten to me, and others, I am
sure, to say leave Anzac Day as it is. Leave Waitangi Day as it is. Let them remain as
days of commemoration. I am proud and happy to not support this bill, and, in doing so,
support our veterans.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: What a privilege to be the last speaker before an
exciting vote is about to take place on th is bill, the Holidays (Full Recognition of
Waitangi Day and ANZAC Day) Amendment Bill. The New Zealand public is about to
get a taste of what it would be like to ha ve a good, pragmatic Labour Government in
place by seeing the sorts of pragmatic bills that would make a difference to hard-
working families in New Zealand. They can  watch this debate this afternoon and go
“Yes, that’s what we’d get under Labour. That’s what we’d get under Labour.”, because
very soon the Government is about to be defeated. The Governme nt is about to be
defeated in about, oh, 5 minutes’ time. I think I might take a short call, just to make sure
it gets defeated a little bit earlier.
It is not before time that that Government gets defeated in its mean-spirited approach
towards working families. That can be the only reason why the National Government is
actually putting itself in the position of being defeated on a bill, because it so does not
want to give families the opportunity every 7 years to have the statutory holidays that
they get every other year. How mean-spirited is that?
I think this bill demonstrates absolute ly for the New Zealand public the big
difference in having a Labour Government  in place, where Labour clearly backs
working families, and clearly backs the idea that we want families to be able to spend
more time together, that we want workers to be well supported, and that we are not
mean-spirited enough to come up with a myri ad of bizarre arguments about why every
seventh year we would rob working families of 2 days off that they get every other year.
There can be just no good argument for that. I think that National has demonstrated that
again today, that there is in fact no good argument for it.
On Anzac Day and Waitangi Day New Zealanders will commemorate those days two
times every 7 years in the same way that they do every other year. The fact that they are
getting the right to have those 11 statutory holidays stay in place is not going to alter
17 Apr 2013 Holidays (Waitangi & Anzac Days) Amdt Bill 9481
that. What it will do is it will mean that they will actually get an opportunity to have
those 11 statutory holidays. We have alrea dy had that debate in New Zealand. The law
has already been passed that says that we have 20 days of  annual leave and we have 11
statutory holidays every year. It is only a quirk in the le gislation that actually stops
Anzac Day and Waitangi Day being celebrated in exactly the same way on those two
times every 7 years. It is mean-spirited for the Government to argue  and actually risk a
defeat in the House over trying to rob workin g families of those two holidays. It just
shows how out of touch it is with ordinary New Zealanders, and it is getting more and
more out of touch every day.
I do feel a sense of connection to this bill because the day—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Oh, it’s your bill now? Oh, that’s right.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: No, she’s a Labour MP.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Yes, it is because I am a Labour MP, so I feel a very strong sense
of connection. But the first reading of this bill happened to be on the same day as the
first reading of the other bill that defeats th e Government, and that is the bill to extend
paid parental leave by 6 months. These two bills started out their journey together. This
bill is coming to fruition an awful lot earlie r than the Parental Leave and Employment
Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill, but as long as we get paid
parental leave extended to families as well, I do not mind the wait.
But I am really, really excited to congratulate two colleagues who have worked very,
very hard on behalf of working families in  New Zealand to make sure that this
legislation gets through this House, and to ma ke sure that that entitlement goes to those
families. One is David Clark, whose name this  bill is in. He has done a fantastic job. He

MP to do. Then there is our deputy leader , Grant Robertson, who actually drafted the
bill initially. He relied on the good luck of  David Clark, who obviously has got the luck
of the Irish—
